items.body:
Ezra Feinberg’s third album Soft Power sees the composer-guitarist enlist an impressive array of fellow musicians including Mary Lattimore, David Moore (Bing & Ruth), Jefre Cantu-Ledesma, and Robbie Lee.

"Defined by its abundance of melodies, repeating figures and ecstatic improvisations, Soft Power exudes an enlightened and transformative spirit to empower the listener. The compassionate, tender-hearted opener ‘Future Sand’ deftly interweaves flutes and steady arpeggios. The Reichian pulse beneath the soaring melody is played not on the customary analogue sequencer, but on finger-picked acoustic guitar, one of the lodestars of Feinberg’s compositional approach. ‘Soft Power’, the buoyant and mesmeric title track that follows builds over a rich bed of guitars and a reverb-y Rhodes melody reminiscent of a Strata East LP, its narrative arc bountiful in energy, optimism and future dreaming, a perfect accompaniment to long days of summertide.

‘Pose Beams’ blends the chamber-jazz approach of Penguin Café Orchestra with a balletic kosmische, climaxing with a galvanising crescendo and “free improv” section performed by fellow New Yorkers - Robbie Lee (piano) and Jefre Cantu-Ledesma, whose granular and modular synths sprinkle particle dust over the expressive drumming of John Thayer. ‘Flutter Intensity’ evokes in part the music of Cluster as played on acoustic guitars, which ping-pong across the stereo field, providing the canvas for a plaintive vibraphone line reminiscent of TNT-era Tortoise. Instruments move in tandem, but also drift and glide allowing them the space to hang in the air, the variegated rhythms, textures, and tones all laced into the fabric of the album.

At the centrefold of the albums 7-tracks is ‘The Big Clock’, a tryptic piece that evolves from pairs of stretched varying tones, creating fields of technicolour over an unabashed motorik beat, serving to offset the pastoral and ambient registers heard elsewhere. It features the first of two appearances from David Moore (Bing & Ruth) who plays lilting piano lines on the come-down. ‘There Was Somebody There’ returns to the album’s earlier wistfulness, a hard stereo-panned soundworld with lightly strummed, interlocking acoustic guitars combining to pigment a washy, painterly scene. David Moore and Jefre Cantu-Ledesma provide reviving synths, the underlying pulse that seems to simulate a life cycle; another day on Earth. The album closes with the reflective ‘Get Some Rest’ featuring Mary Lattimore, whose harp pluckings set a dreamlike tone against bare organic acoustics and flourishing flutes to create a sense of realignment and restoration.

Feinberg artfully transcends the listener to an enriched place, his compositions distinguished by the deep humanity that lies at their core, plugging the listener into a state of wide eyed being, open and alive. Soft Power then is Ezra’s own mantra but also one of power giving - a colourful catharsis translated into music. Feinberg’s music always speaks to the listener, but Soft Power, in whispering, speaks loudest."

items.body: In April 2025, Argentinian, Brooklyn-based pianist Leo Genovese just finished a concert with The Mars Volta at Madison Square Garden and had ninety free minutes before the tour bus would move on. He called his friends - Japanese, Tokyo-based double bass player (and cellist) Takeshi Sugawa, one of the busiest musicians in the Japanese scene, leader of his Banksia trio, who hosted Genovese in his debut album as bandleader ( Outgrowing , 2018, with drummer Tom Rainey), who was in New York as part of the Satoko Fujii Tokyo Trio North American tour, and Australian drummer Alfred Vogel, of How Noisy Are the Rooms? And Vanish trios, the founder of Boomslang Records and the Bezau Beatz festival, who was visiting New York and had previously recorded with Genovese ( Eyes to the Sun , Boomslang, 2024, with fellow Argentinian sax player Camila Nebbia). Sugawa and Vogel did not know each other, and the ad hoc trio met for dinner in a small restaurant and immediately felt the need to play together. Genovese, Sugawa, and Vogel promised each other that they had to repeat this experience. It did not take long. In May 2025, Genovese played in Berlin with Esperanza Spalding, Sugawa was touring in Europe, and Vogel booked the Bonello Studio in Berlin for an all-night, free-improvised recording session that produced Unleashed . The music is quite spacious and understated, sketching its movement with delicate, skeletal strokes, without a plan and with no aim of reaching cohesive structures or grooves, as if asking the listener to be an active part of its creation and imagine where it can land. Genovese, Sugawa, and Vogel are attuned to every sound and gesture, as each one opens more sonic threads, but without attaching themselves to any of them. Melodic veins rise and dissolve organically, but the deep listening, deeply poetic, spontaneous, primal, and collective, egalitarian process is the essence of this trio. The trio distills its dynamics on the poetic, 13-minute “A World of One Colour”. Letting go and just being in the moment when everything opens, or, as Sugawa puts it, “A spirit that wanders, that lives across times and places.” Hopefully, Genovese, Sugawa, and Vogel would find time in their busy schedules to take this trio on the road, letting it blossom even more on a tight tour. UNLEASHED by Leo Genovese, Takashi Sugawa, Alfred Vogel Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: Label: Sunnyside Records, 2026 Personnel - Co Streiff: alto saxophone; Russ Johnson: trumpet; Christian Weber: double bass; Gerry Hemingway: drums. Swiss saxophonist Co Streiff and American trumpeter Russ Johnson join forces once again on Oracle , a six-track date where both bring their imaginative, open compositions to the fore. 15 years after In Circles , the pair—backed by the cooperative rhythm team of bassist Christian Weber and seasoned drummer Gerry Hemingway (replacing Julius Sartorius)—is back in action. Despite the recording hiatus, the band got together in 2019, developing further ties that culminated in a 2023 tour. Johnson’s “ Horizontal Heartburn ”, initially a vehicle for Hemingway’s balance of dry and wet toms and syncopated hi-hat pulsation, follows with dramatic shifts in urgency, tension, and release. A staccato-driven section pumped up with unison horn lines soon morphs into a lyrically conscious theme contoured by tone-center shifts. Johnson’s noble way of articulating phrases is substantiated over sturdy bass plucks, and the piece soon engages in marching steps, leading to a frantic final dance. Streiff’s “ Smithy Street ” invites us to a funk-rock groove, perfectly suitable for measured avant-garde considerations. The saxophonist also contributes “ Remember Little Feather ”, a free-bop swing ride where she adds clever motifs, taking us to Ornette Coleman and Don Cherry. The tempo rises to double time for Johnson’s adrenaline-infused statement, with Hemingway stealing the spotlight at the end as he embarks on climactic rhythmic tapestries overflowing with interesting ideas. While the final track, “ Oracle ”, offers a creatively bluesy atmosphere, Johnson’s “ Sanguache ” comes shrouded in a cool vibe enhanced by nonchalant parallel melodies and a strong, hi-hat-accentuated backbeat. This tune preserves its lyrical side even when the band makes a somewhat unexpected turn into rock. One of the strongest pieces consists of a combination of Streiff’s “ In Circles ”, first recorded on the previous album, and Johnson’s “ Yellow Crane ”. Warm bluesy colors, a breezy tone, and an uncluttered rhythmic texture emerge with a 3/4 feel. Weber’s excellent skills and attention to detail make the transition to the chamber-jazz painterliness of the second tune, which enters in reflection mode with foundational bowed bass maneuvers. Oracle provides an effective sonic canvas, showcasing the distinctive chemistry between these two leaders and the depth of what they can create together. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Horizontal Heartburn ► 03 - In Circles / Yellow Crane ► 05 - Remember Little Feather

items.body:
Voices of Singapore Youth Choir (VYC) has made history as the first Singaporean choir to win a Grand Prix on the Asia Choral Grand Prix circuit.

The ensemble took home the top prize at the 2026 Malaysian International Choral Eisteddfod (MCE), held from 19 to 23 August in Kuala Lumpur. The competition brought together around 220 choirs from around the world, including ensembles from Russia, Kosovo, and across Asia.

On 22 August, VYC fielded 72 singers in the Mixed Choir category (A5), joined by the Voices of Singapore Children’s Choir’s Choral Scholars. The ensemble earned Gold and was named Category Winner with a score of 93.2 — the highest score recorded at the festival.

The Choral Scholars also competed separately in the Teenage category (A3), fielding 42 singers and securing Gold and the Category Winner title with a score of 91.00, the festival’s second-highest score.

Both ensembles subsequently advanced to the Grand Prix round on 23 August, where they competed alongside nine other choirs for the festival’s overall title. VYC emerged as Grand Prix Champion, marking the first time a Singaporean choir has claimed a Grand Prix at one of the competitions on the Asia Choral Grand Prix circuit.

“It is incredibly surreal, and an immensely proud moment for Singapore as we showcase the excellence of Singapore’s choral music-making on the international stage,” said Dr Darius Lim, Founder and Artistic Director of Voices of Singapore.

“This achievement does not belong to just one choir. It belongs to our entire choral community and, in many ways, to our country,” he added, crediting the conductors, music educators, and voice teachers who have supported the singers over the years.

The Malaysian International Choral Eisteddfod is one of five competitions on the Asia Choral Grand Prix circuit, alongside the Andrea O. Veneracion International Choral Festival in the Philippines, Bali International Choir Festival in Indonesia, Singapore International Choral Festival, and Korea International Choir Competition.

Following its win, VYC will represent MCE at the next Asia Choral Grand Prix in Manila, held in conjunction with the Andrea O. Veneracion International Choral Festival. There, the Singaporean ensemble will go up against fellow Grand Prix winners from across the circuit for the Asia Choral Grand Prix Cup.

The milestone adds to Voices of Singapore’s previous successes at MCE. VOS Men and VOS City Chorus have both earned Gold awards at the competition, while VOS Men was also named a Category Winner. This latest victory, however, marks the first overall Grand Prix title for a Voices of Singapore choir at the festival.

items.body:
Khalid is making his way back to Bangkok! The multi-platinum singer-songwriter is set to bring his It’s Always Summer Somewhere Tour on 29 November to UOB LIVE, Emsphere, following a run of sold-out shows across 23 cities on the tour’s U.S. leg.

For his Bangkok return, fans can expect a career-spanning set that brings together Khalid’s signature mix of R&B, pop, and soul. The announced selection includes fan favourites and global hits such as 'Location', 'Young Dumb & Broke', 'Better', 'Talk', 'Love Lies', and 'Eastside', alongside material from his latest musical chapter.

The tour takes its inspiration from Khalid’s latest album, After the Sun Goes Down. Released in October 2025, the 17-track record blends smooth R&B with electro-pop and ‘80s-inspired synths, and features the singles 'In Plain Sight' and 'Nah'. The project marked a new chapter for the artist following his third album, Sincere.

Since breaking through with 'Location', Khalid has gone on to amass more than 35.6 billion streams globally and seven GRAMMY nominations. His catalogue also includes collaborations with Normani, Halsey, Benny Blanco, Billie Eilish, Ed Sheeran, Alicia Keys, and Marshmello. More recently, he worked with Oskar Med K on 'Nobody (Make Me Feel)' and with KYGO and Griffyn on 'Save My Love'.

Tickets are now available via Ticketmaster Thailand.

items.body:
Beerfest Asia is heading to the beach for its next chapter.

Happening from 11 to 13 September, BFA @ The Beach will take over Palawan Green, Sentosa for three days of music, beer, global flavours, and community experiences. Presented by Tiger®, the reimagined festival will bring together more than 180 beers alongside international food offerings and a music programme featuring over 22 acts.

Positioned as the beginning of "BFA 2.0," the festival will centre on a new organising principle — Community × Discovery × Lifestyle Culture. While beer remains at its core, this edition is expanding the Beerfest Asia experience beyond the drink itself, with food and music serving as additional ways for different communities to come together.

"When we started BFA 2.0, the question wasn’t simply how to put Beerfest Asia on again. It was why Beerfest Asia should exist and what purpose it could serve," shared Festival Director Paul Lee.

"Community, Discovery and Lifestyle Culture became our answer. We want to bring people together, give Singapore’s brewers a stronger platform and create a place where different communities, cultures and flavours can meet."

From emo and K-pop DJs to ‘80s, ‘90s and 2000s favourites

For music fans, BFA @ The Beach is building its weekend soundtrack around Mixtape Memories, a programme spanning the defining music of the 1980s, 1990s and 2000s alongside contemporary sounds and emerging acts.

More than 22 acts comprising live bands, international DJs, community performances, emerging artists, and sunset acoustic sessions will perform across the weekend, with Singapore artists joined by acts from the Philippines and South Korea.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Beerfest Asia (@beerfestasia)

Among the international names is Filipino band SUD, who will make an exclusive showcase at the festival.

South Korea will also be represented by DJ Ina, a K-pop idol turned DJ whose sets move through EDM, bounce, house, and techno, as well as DJ Tigger, whose career stretches back to Seoul's club scene in the 1990s. The latter has worked as a music director for Club CHAV and Club COCOON, founded DJ label Soul Papa, and formed producing duo Tigger & Giovani.

Closer to home, Saturday night will turn up the nostalgia with the EMONIGHTSG LIVE EXPERIENCE. Since 2016, EMONIGHTSG has built a following around emo, pop-punk, alternative rock, and nu-metal anthems from the likes of Paramore, My Chemical Romance, and Jimmy Eat World.

The collective has previously brought its sing-and-scream parties to F1 Singapore, Baybeats, and the Singapore Rugby Sevens, while also hosting guest performances from touring artists including Yellowcard and Silverstein. Its BFA @ The Beach appearance will include a DJ set by THEBRYANSTATE from 9:30 PM on Saturday.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Beerfest Asia (@beerfestasia)

Elsewhere, the lineup will tap into plenty of throwback favourites. Rock Rosettes will pay tribute to Paramore, No Doubt, and Alanis Morissette, while TABULA & Friends will revisit music from Foo Fighters, Oasis, The Killers, and more.

Kabin Krue will take on favourites from Bryan Adams, Goo Goo Dolls, and Metallica, while Velvet Typhoon will bring Mando and Canto classics from the likes of BEYOND and A-SHIN into the mix.

The festival's trip through music history will continue with Happy Together, performing tributes to Spice Girls, Take That, Hanson, and more; Ruby Rocks, taking on Green Day, Nirvana, and Jet; and The Unfortunate Sons, celebrating Creedence Clearwater Revival.

Inertia will bring alternative rock favourites including Coldplay and Counting Crows, while Slytra Trio will take on Lady Gaga anthems. Bushmen, meanwhile, will deliver classic reggae mixtapes, while Jacklyn, Juni & Cheng will revisit classic Mandopop hits.

Also on the bill are Shane Low, with tributes spanning Michael Jackson, Matchbox Twenty, and Robbie Williams; Kamadooma, bringing beach-ready grooves and sunset singalongs; and international school band EIT Project.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Beerfest Asia (@beerfestasia)

On the decks, DJ Maverick, DJ Timo, and DJ Victor will revisit old-school hip-hop, ‘90s pop, and retro favourites, while DJ Saud will bring a Gen Z spin with his mixtapes.

The performances will unfold around a 360-degree omnidirectional main stage designed with gathering and shared experiences in mind. A separate Sunset Stage will provide acoustic sounds by the beach, taking festival-goers from the afternoon through golden hour and into the evening.

More than 180 beers from Singapore and around the world

Music is only one part of the expanded BFA experience.

With Tiger® serving as Title Sponsor and Official Beer, BFA @ The Beach will put Singapore's brewing story front and centre. The homegrown beer brand, which was born in Singapore in 1932, is now available in more than 60 markets worldwide.

Alongside it will be a new generation of Singapore brewers, including The 1925 Brewing Co., Sunbird Brewing Company, Rainforest Brewery, People People Brewing Co., Rye & Pint, and RedDot BrewHouse, among others. People People Brewing Co. will also serve as the festival's Official Craft Beer.

The festival is using that homegrown lineup to look beyond simply sampling beers, raising larger questions around what defines a Singapore beer, how local breweries can grow in a small and high-cost market, and how heritage, provenance, and Asian palates can help build a distinctive local brewing identity.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Beerfest Asia (@beerfestasia)

Those conversations are also set to inform BREWED HERE, a proposed three-part vodcast series with official media partners The Peak and HardwareZone. The series is envisioned around three themes — Identity, Economics, and Legacy — exploring Singapore craft beer through the wider lenses of entrepreneurship, family enterprise, differentiation, survival, and succession.

The local breweries will meet an extensive international selection at Palawan Green. More than 180 beers from markets including China, Taiwan, Vietnam, Estonia, Germany, France, Scandinavia, and beyond will be represented.

For the first time at Beerfest Asia, the Brewers Association will also participate, bringing beers from more than eight independent American craft breweries to Singapore.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Beerfest Asia (@beerfestasia)

Global flavours meet Singapore craft beer

Food will be another major part of the discovery experience, with flavours drawing from Germany, Mexico, Korea, Thailand, Italy, Japan, and more.

One of the festival's most curated food-and-beer experiences will be Sunset Social, helmed by Executive Chef Dexter Ko of Creative Eateries.

Ko will create 12 canapés around beers from three selected Singapore breweries. Inspired by BFA @ The Beach's tropical setting, the menu will explore how qualities such as freshness, fruitiness, spice, acidity, richness, aroma, and texture interact with different beers.

Rather than approaching the experience as a straightforward beer-and-food pairing, Sunset Social is designed to bring the curiosity commonly associated with wine pairing to Singapore craft beer and tropical flavours.

A new home for Beerfest Asia

The shift to Palawan Green is also central to the festival's wider reset.

Located along Sentosa's beachfront with open sea views, the green space is intended to give Beerfest Asia something it previously lacked: a consistent sense of place from which the festival can develop its identity and relationship with its audience.

Planning for the first BFA @ The Beach began only in late April and early May, giving organisers around four months to develop the new strategy, establish its new home, build partnerships, engage local and international brewers, and put together the festival.

According to Lee, this September's edition is consequently being viewed as the starting point rather than the finished form of BFA 2.0.

"Four months is a very tight timeline to start building a new festival, and we are realistic about what can be achieved in one edition," he said.

"What matters is that we start with purpose. We can give Singapore’s brewers a stronger platform, put them alongside brewing cultures from around the world and bring different communities together through food, music and shared experiences."

He added: "Great festivals are built over time. They develop traditions, communities and a relationship with a place. This September is about laying those foundations — not simply to stage another Beerfest Asia, but to start building a new festival for Singapore."

Responsible drinking and sustainability

The festival's broader approach to beer culture will include measures around responsible drinking and sustainability.

BFA @ The Beach will operate a Challenge 21 age-verification policy alongside responsible alcohol service, food, and hydration. Heineken 0.0 will be the Official No/Lo Beer, while Montana Alps will serve as the Official Hydration Partner.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Beerfest Asia (@beerfestasia)

Every Discovery Pass will also come with The Discovery Mug, a reusable 330ml frosty mug designed to keep beverages chilled without ice. Festival-goers can use the mug throughout BFA @ The Beach before taking it home afterwards.

The festival also arrives amid a growing conversation around beer tourism in Asia. A forthcoming research report from Beer Asia is set to examine the region's potential for beer tourism and how breweries, festivals, and local beer cultures could shape travellers' experiences of destinations.

For BFA @ The Beach, Singapore's combination of international connectivity, culinary diversity, hospitality, compact geography, and position at the crossroads of Asia forms part of that proposition — bringing local brewers together with international beer and food cultures in one tropical destination.

Further brewery, food, entertainment, partnership, and festival announcements are expected ahead of BFA @ The Beach.

items.body: Improvisations for the Land proceeds with unusual patience. Alessandro Ciccarelli and Milena Punzi Anfossi never seem in a hurry to introduce new material. Instead, they linger over individual sounds, allowing them to exhaust their possibilities before searching for another direction. At several points the music appears to reach an impasse, only for one of the musicians to uncover an entirely new path from within the same sonic terrain. The three improvisations share this quality of persistence, probing ever deeper where it might seem there is nothing left to uncover. The relationship between analogue synthesizer and electric cello is one of constant adjustment. Neither instrument occupies a permanent foreground. Sometimes the synthesizer holds a low-frequency plateau almost stubbornly while the cello slowly alters its pressure, grain and register around it. Elsewhere the electronics recede almost completely, leaving bowed textures to define the pace before quietly reclaiming the space through sustained drones and subtle shifts in colour. The music rarely advances through contrast. It moves by patiently examining the consequences of each gesture. Trial-and-error and risk-taking shape the entire album. High frequencies are sometimes sustained long enough to become physically demanding, forcing the listener to remain inside their unsettling presence instead of treating them as fleeting accents. Low drones establish a bodily weight that occasionally feels architectural rather than harmonic. Even when the texture thickens, each sound retains its own presence, allowing the ear to follow the gradual redistribution of energy across the spectrum. Listening repeatedly, one becomes increasingly aware of how carefully the musicians resist resolution. Electronic textures are allowed to stall. Bowed sounds lose energy without being replaced. Instead of smoothing over moments of uncertainty, Ciccarelli and Punzi Anfossi remain with them, allowing hesitation and suspension to become productive musical states. There is a quiet confidence in this willingness to stay with a sound after it has apparently reached its destination. The titles inevitably invite historical associations. Named after Palestinian villages destroyed during the Nakba, the three improvisations carry an emotional and political charge that extends beyond the music itself. Yet, as the musicians explain in the accompanying interview, the names were chosen only after the recordings had been completed. They do not function as narratives but acknowledge a state of mind that accompanied the project. The music retains its autonomy while remaining inseparable from the experiences that shaped its creation. The cover artwork quietly reinforces this idea. Its layered aerial image shows a fractured landscape at different degrees of resolution and density. Surfaces overlap, traces emerge only to disappear beneath new textures, and the eye is left to make sense of the jagged terrain. It mirrors the music’s own behaviour: sounds accumulate through successive layers, preserving earlier gestures without ever allowing them to become fixed. There is no attempt to overwhelm the listener through density or technical display. The album asks for a different kind of attention, one willing to remain inside slowly evolving textures and to follow sounds beyond their apparent destination. The longer one spends with these improvisations, the more they reveal through the patient excavation of what was already there. That patient search gives Improvisations for the Land its own voice. photo by Leonardo Chiarabini – The Factory PRD To explore things further, we have reached out to Alessandro Ciccarelli and Milena Punzi Anfossi. Improvisations for the Land is rooted in free improvisation, yet the album is also explicitly dedicated to Palestine, with each piece named after a village destroyed during the Nakba in 1948. Rather than illustrating specific events, the music seems to inhabit a space of tension, absence, and attentive listening. How did the decision to name the pieces after Isdud, Jusayr, and Hulayqat shape the improvisations themselves? Were you thinking about these places while performing, or did their historical weight become part of the music retrospectively? We believe that instrumental music — and, more specifically, the kind of improvisational practice we pursue — belongs to a process of abstraction in which music both can and should represent nothing but itself, rather than describing or illustrating events, images, or narratives. This autonomy, however, does not justify the notion of an art detached from life. On the contrary, life itself, the events that surround us, and the history we live through inevitably permeate our being, our sensibilities, and our actions as individuals and as musicians. For this reason, although sound does not represent anything, it is never a neutral or sterile space. As John Cage famously said, “Everything we do is music.” The world therefore does not remain outside music; it inevitably enters it through those who create it and those who listen. In his writings on music, Edward Said consistently defended the formal rigor of classical music without ever separating it from his condition as a Palestinian intellectual living in exile. For him, these two dimensions were never in conflict; they coexisted within the same gesture. The autonomy of form does not entail amnesia on the part of those who practice it. With this in mind, the titles of these pieces are neither captions nor interpretative keys, nor do they ask the listener to search within the music for references to a place or event. In her essay “Against Interpretation,” Susan Sontag argued that interpretation can become a way of taming a work of art — reducing it to its content and then interpreting that, making it manageable. At a time when criticism tended to approach every work as something to decode, the first question became, “What does it mean?”— as though its value lay in some hidden message waiting to be extracted and restated elsewhere. For Sontag, this is precisely what taming means: neutralizing what is intrinsic to a work, what cannot be reduced to a concept, in order to render it harmless. At bottom, this is what she calls “the philistine refusal to leave the work of art alone.” Interpretation risked extinguishing the immediate, sensory impact that a work has on those who hear or see it — an experience that is essential and prior to any content one might later extract from it. We therefore conceive these titles not as content to be extracted from the music, but as biographical traces of ourselves. They do not assign meaning to the listening experience; rather, they point to those who made the music. The decision to title and dedicate these pieces to villages destroyed during the Nakba came only afterward, once the music already existed, but not in order to impose an external meaning upon it. Rather, it was an acknowledgment that those improvisations had already been traversed by our own anxieties, by the anger and grief we felt in the face of the unspeakable. The title does not explain the music; it names the condition of those who created it. Isdud 1930 In the liner notes you write that, while art cannot stop violence, it also cannot remain isolated from the world. That raises a broader question about artistic responsibility. When working on an entirely improvised album, how do you negotiate the relationship between political intention and musical openness? Were there moments where you felt the music itself resisted the conceptual framework you had established, or did improvisation become precisely the right language for responding to events that seem almost impossible to represent? Free improvisation is probably the musical practice in which the performer’s life, emotions, thoughts, and memories enter the musical act most directly. Not by narrating events, but by allowing the sound itself to reveal a presence of one’s inner world that precedes any explanation. Unlike composed music, the outcome of improvisation is always bound to the hic et nunc of the self, and of the self in relation to the other. The environment, one’s state of mind, one’s thoughts, and interpersonal relationships are all integral to the construction of the music. They do not constitute an external context; they are among the very materials of improvisation. For Christopher Small, music is not so much an object as a shared activity — a process of musicking that encompasses performers, listeners, and the relationships that emerge between them in the moment of performance. If there is a political dimension, it is enacted within this network of relationships that comes into being every time people make music together. Pauline Oliveros described Deep Listening as the practice of “listening in every possible way to everything possible to hear.” For us, this means that improvisation is not merely about producing sounds, but about assuming the responsibility of being fully present: listening to one another, to the space, and to the world. It is a mode of listening that precedes expressive intention and also entails a willingness to be transformed by whatever unfolds. For this reason, we have never experienced any tension between political commitment and musical openness. As we suggested earlier, lived experience inevitably enters the sound itself, and precisely for that reason we believe free improvisation is the language best suited to engaging with events that exceed every possibility of representation. Faced with tragedies of this magnitude, music neither can nor should claim to narrate, explain, or stand in for history. What it can do is become a space in which such experiences continue to question both those who perform and those who listen. According to Jacques Rancière, the politics of art does not reside in the message it conveys, but in the way it reconfigures the distribution of the sensible — that is, what can be seen, heard, and shared. In a complementary sense, Jacques Attali argued that music is prophecy: rather than merely reflecting society, it heralds forms that have not yet become visible elsewhere, in a movement he calls annunciatory. If this is true, then a record such as this does not simply “comment” on tragedy through its titles. Rather, in the very way it is organized and experienced, it attempts to imagine a different configuration of reality. For this reason, we do not believe in the possibility of neutral art. The autonomy of music does not mean isolation from history. Every sonic gesture emerges within a network of relationships, experiences, and responsibilities. In this sense, it is not so much that music “speaks about politics”; rather, sound itself, as a human gesture situated in the world, inevitably possesses a political dimension. Sound is political. Hulayqat 1940s map Compared to your previous duo album All’improvviso, the instrumentation here has been reduced to its bare essentials: electric cello and analogue synthesizer. Yet that apparent limitation produces an extraordinarily rich sonic vocabulary, where it often becomes difficult to distinguish which sounds belong to the cello and which emerge from the synthesizer. How has your musical dialogue evolved since your first collaboration, and what possibilities did this more austere instrumental setup open up for both of you? We both share the need to constantly question ourselves and to explore new ways of discovering sound within sound. This happens both individually, through our own personal research, and collectively in our work as a duo. By “new means” we do not simply refer to different devices or instruments, as was the case with our first album, All’Improvviso, but also to new expressive possibilities that emerge from a deeper exploration of each instrument itself. Sometimes, innovation does not come from adding new elements, but from looking more deeply at what is already available to us and questioning our habitual ways of using it. Our decision to reduce the instrumentation to an electric cello and an analogue synthesizer was therefore not an act of renunciation, but part of this very process: a way of focusing our attention on sonic material itself. Limiting our means — both in terms of instruments and musical materials — has never felt like a constraint. On the contrary, it creates a deeper space for exploration, where every timbral variation, every resonance, and every subtle detail acquires greater significance. Giacinto Scelsi spoke of the profondeur du son — the depth of sound — conceiving sound not merely as a vehicle for music but as an autonomous universe to be explored in its own internal complexity. From this perspective, our interest is not simply in combining the electric cello and the analogue synthesizer as two distinct instruments, but in exploring the point at which their identities begin to dissolve and sound becomes a shared space, a material in continuous transformation. This exploration unfolds through a process of exchange and reciprocity, ideally reaching a point where the distinction between the two sound sources no longer matters. The fact that it is often difficult to tell whether a particular sound originates from the cello or the synthesizer is therefore not merely the result of each of us pursuing our own timbral research. Rather, it is the outcome of an encounter between two depths: both instruments become generators of a shared sonic material, continuously transformed through listening, interaction, and mutual responsiveness. Jusair 1940s map Listening to Improvisations for the Land, I was struck by how much the music relies on restraint. Silence, resonance, and microscopic changes in timbre often carry as much expressive weight as the more overt musical gestures, while the dialogue between electric cello and analogue synthesizer unfolds with remarkable patience and responsiveness. At many points it becomes difficult to tell where one instrument ends and the other begins, as both seem to inhabit the same evolving sonic space. How do you cultivate that degree of mutual listening during improvisation? Is it something that develops over years of playing together, or do you deliberately create conditions that allow unexpected musical relationships to emerge in the moment? Although a musical relationship can certainly be built and deepened over time through shared experience and growing familiarity, there are also rare encounters in which something seems to happen immediately, before words and without the need for any particular preparation. These are the moments when a musical dialogue emerges from the very first sound, as a form of mutual recognition. That epiphany is exactly what happened the first time we played together as a duo. All’improvviso, our first album, grew out of that experience: a first meeting, with no rehearsal, no predetermined structures, and no direction established in advance. We simply brought our willingness to listen and to respond to whatever unfolded in the present moment. Ever since that first encounter, we have had the feeling that our shared sound has always found its own continuity, its own direction, while remaining completely open. Of course, this sense of affinity does not imply the absence of research or risk. On the contrary, within such a deep mode of listening, the unexpected becomes an essential source of creative energy. What we do not know is not an obstacle but an opportunity for transformation. Improvisation ultimately lives within this tension between familiarity and the unknown. Writing about non-idiomatic improvisation, Derek Bailey argued that the value of this practice lies precisely in not knowing in advance what will happen. It is not defined by the absence of an idiom, but by the decision to relinquish any pre-existing idiom in order to remain in the position of discovering something together with another person. We recognize the foundation of our own listening to one another in that condition, more than in any acquired technique. For us, improvisation means exposing ourselves to the risk of losing what we already know, accepting that control can never be total, and allowing space for something that can emerge only through the relationship itself. It is precisely this dimension of risk that keeps the musical dialogue alive and vital. In this sense, listening is not simply the ability to follow the other; it is also the willingness to allow the other to change the course of our own path. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.album: Dean De Benedictis :: Salvaging The Future (Spotted Peccary Music)
items.excerpt: With the completion of this trilogy, we acknowledge our part as a remote viewer of Dean’s life over three decades. items.body: With the completion of this trilogy, we acknowledge our part as a remote viewer of Dean’s life over three decades. Salvaging The Future—perhaps more than the prior two albums—is a restless collage, yet it is so well mixed that it lends itself to uninterrupted full-album listening. This listener is tuning in about 2x per day at the moment. Despite the challenges these decades have wrought, the trilogy’s close with “Our Story Survives Collectively” leaves us with a sense of hope. This is music for visioning. Revolutionizing the human listening experience Salvaging The Future by Dean De Benedictis Salvaging the Future utilizes electronic mastery alongside sparse traditional acoustic instruments and vocals to revolutionize the human listening experience. There will be no undisturbed sleeping, only optional vivid, deep-set dreaming. Music that completely upends your expectations can feel like a sensory assault on the first spin, but the feeling soon becomes mostly energizing and sustaining, including a wispy blend of limitless and beatless space signatures, as well as beat inspired enchantment. This is Art, intending to allow the unconscious mind to somehow express itself, often resulting in the depiction of illogical or dreamlike scenes and ideas. “Moving forward with mindfulness would quite literally mean salvaging the future,” offers De Benedictis. We may expect The Future to bring about profound changes in our listening arts through universal joyfulness, mindful that nothing is forever. As for dancing, that is up to you. I seek a collage shifting into every new world imaginable, or mostly never before imagined. Southern California-based artist Dean De Benedictis has delivered an absolute masterpiece for your collection of auditory journeys that completely bypass conventional reason and transport your mind into uncharted, supernatural territories. He ​is widely recognized in the electronic ambient community as Surface 10. Surface 10 has a long history with performing at galactic electronic music festivals as well as releasing his solo and collaborative recordings internationally, such as on the DiN label, Hypnotic, Space For Music, as well as some self-released works. His previous work with Spotted Peccary Music includes a collaborative project called Desensitized, with Deborah Martin (Hemispherica Portalis, 2020, and Chaos In Premonition, 2022) as well as two solo albums, Salvaging the Past (2005) and Salvaging the Present (2016). Only optional vivid, deep-set dreaming :: Salvaging the Future presents an attempt to conceive and apply a good degree of futurism to every aspect of its creation. From sound design, to instrumentation, to compositional production, perhaps one way to see it (or hear it) is as an illusive combination of progressive and contemporary influences that all “tap the future on the shoulder” or if nothing else, maybe exchange a hat-tip to that which is to come. Additionally, the obvious suggestion that humanity’s future may still have hope for survival and even thriving; that we may somehow redeem and persevere not by forgetting or dismissing our weight of the past, but acknowledging and accounting for life experiences as a strategy for our progress ahead. “Aside from representing phases of my life, the Salvaging series began as one idea, and ended as another,” confides De Benedictis. “The musical style of Salvaging The Future follows the suggestion of its inherent theme: a wild departure from most past and current genres, diving head first into hyper-forward approaches, perhaps in some ways “of the future.” “I would produce and perform music in harsh desert planes, steep canyons, mountainsides and summits, windswept shores and forested wilderness; I would work in abandoned buildings, housing construction, airplane flights, cafes, hotels, museums, libraries, or while staying with friends, family, or indeed at home, which was most of the time even if not by far. I tended to do a lot of re-synth types of methods, so found sounds combined with both customized sample libraries and Apple libraries were yet again the main source of instrumentation on Salvaging The Future, much like Salvaging The Present.” Also, like Salvaging The Present, there was an immense amount of processor stacking and automation, mountains of hardware, on every instrument track. “Featured on both albums was also a customized library of drum hits I created in 2014, in which each hit captures the reverb trail-from a note (or harmony) that was sung just before it. This hit library formulated a fairly unmistakable signature-sound in most of my work that followed. I still use that custom-drum-hits library to this day. However, unlike Salvaging The Present, which was completely produced on only one laptop, Salvaging The Future was composed on my first two laptops as well as my first tower. It was all old Apple gear and software, but for some reason that still sounded better to me than some of my newer gear and software, so I decided to just accept the old-system setbacks and finish the album on those devices regardless. A wild departure from most past and current genres :: “It almost broke me. I had to deal with endless system complications on every device, prompting constant work-arounds with Logic and Ableton, but the sound made it worthwhile for me.” De Benedictis continues his long, internationally recognized history of stripping ordinary objects of their normal significance to expose deep psychological truths. By tying an essential common thread between opposing genres, he has created an abstract, emotionally rich masterwork that demands to be heard for fans of avant-garde electronic exploration. Salvaging the Future was composed, performed, mixed, edited, designed and conceptualized by Dean De Benedictis between 2010 and 2025, using mostly software on laptops. His additional instruments were flute, voice, piano and guitar. Production locations were scattered throughout the US west coast but based primarily in Thousand Oaks and Santa Monica, CA. Contributing extra recorded musicians, in addition to Apple loops, include: Lara De Benedictis (vocals), D’Von Charley (vocals and native flute), Nichole Michelle Jones (vocals), Lisa Claire Mitterer (vocals), Phil Williams (electric guitar), and various ASMR artists. ASMRtists. Autonomous Sensory Meridian Response (ASMR) and Ray Kersweil’s futurist theory of the Singularity are two unrelated ideas I came across while researching this music, both have been popular but I have never before heard of them, so kudos. ASMR seems to explore some of the physical psychology of sound. The Kersweil concepts are set in the future, during the coming singularity, and all planets and celestial bodies are now shifting and morphing and changing as that same singularity. This revolutionary sonic journey begins abruptly with “My Love Is An Extinction Event” (6:10), a track whose song title invokes the concept of a rapid, widespread drop in biodiversity. Here things come together and things come apart and sometimes this happens at the same time, spinning and bouncing, falling and transferring velocity, which feels bizarre, unbelievable, dreamlike and leads into very strange restless ear-born images. The kind that will change your life. At one moment the mood goes from feeling frenetic to feeling incredibly alive and layered. This unexpected salad of situations, places, or emotional moments that seem detached from everyday reality or logic all feel pretty good, the intimate links between freeing imagination and the mind, and liberation from repressive and archaic social structures. In the beginning, deep space has no beat. Welcome to “The Outer Links”  (6:31). Coming from an intentionally beatless expanse designed to liberate the imagination, giving the listener the sensation of flying through colorful lights, and maneuvering deliberately to liberate the imagination. We are flying along at a more rapid speed now. The feeling is all about bright stars and a sense of transit. Soon everything is almost flying apart and the beat is going at a fast clip. As the album progresses, we encounter “Voca”  (3:35), where small pieces suddenly click and morph into a fast-paced, jamming run driven by a sexy bassline and seasonably hot drum tones. Perhaps the tempo is a bit fidgety but always rich in tone and interesting in context, jumping into many places to tell the story. I do not understand the punchline, but even real life itself can be strange and even uncomfortable when seeking sustenance. Music for visioning :: I think the fourth track starts in a calm memory palace illuminated with tall marble columns, with big bright halls and stairways. Soon a beat contraption comes together and the vocalists start to arrive. “They Fought To Sway” (7:18) is my personal favorite here, the vocals reach a place I have never heard before, and I like that. “Urband Glacier Fund”  (6:27) is probably holding a hidden message, leading to speculation about that extra d in Urband. Hidden portals bring delight, I think that we are in outer space coming upon some new life forms, our synthesizers are carefully subtle and fully capable. Now a new beat arrives and takes over, a new darkness has surrounded the cabin. Are there glaciers in outer space? The flute is here to take us along, with amazing high energy. Now we encounter a big cinematic sly beat and things are happening all over the place, very exciting. “ASMR Tragedy Lines” (6:44) seems to take place down in a very deep tunnel or cavern, robots are building things quietly, except for this one guy. It gets extremely quiet out here, where we are in the cavern. The perception distorts, morphs, and transforms ordinary objects and forms into strange and uncanny variations of themselves. Down there something is always sparkling. Now the whispers in the darkness take over. I keep straining to hear what the voices are planning next. The imaginary narrative shifts beautifully on “Salvaging My Story” (7:12), a track full of radiant stars, choirs, and unexpected juxtapositions that exercise the grand element of surprise. Let’s go out into the fields at night where the space ships will land, be sure to keep an eye out. There are steam powered machines running, there are crickets and I expect to find the children of the night out here. Soon there is a change. There is a shy melodic tune lingering in the caverns along with the choirs and radiant stars. Soon all of the details start coming into focus, this is a big story with plenty of flying at night. Away we are going, exercising the element of surprise, unexpected juxtapositions and non sequitur. It works. This leads right into the slow-burning sunrise of “Future Incandescence” (6:32) which unfolds like a long slow transit in deep space. Now the pace is slower and the feeling is starker, disorienting, with the hallucinatory quality of a dream. There is a language of fragments that flow together and make the whole sound. We are still on the ship, snug inside a safe metal box that is still moving, the closest star is emerging from an eclipse, there are emotions and suspense, there is tension building. The natural world takes a surreal turn on “All The Wild” (4:27), where there are strange gumblings coming from animals that I cannot see. We are all probably back in the big cave again, at night. This time with strange recordings of birds and wildlife playing in the darkness. The variety of strange sounds increases as new species come floating into our range. There are a lot of creatures heard here, such as birds or lizards cooing, insects clicking and humming. I think I hear a synth glowing, perhaps a swan, with pianos and choirs and sustained tones echoing about. Some loons explode or just fly ahead, and there are more new strange creatures. There are whales in our cave here, along with the strings and wings. “Born Of Flight” (7:09) starts in quiet secrecy before combusting into a galloping drum kit that soon clicks like a flying train, keeping the listener in a state of perpetual, blissful motion. We love our cave, it goes on forever. By the end we are clicking like a sleeping railroad carriage, always feeling motion, until we gently float into the close. The album concludes with a magnificent nine-minute epic, “Our Story Survives Collectively” (9:15), and to start we are following our guide into the well lit tunnel or hallway, there are echoes and lots of space above. There are interesting odd vocals, some with a trilling vibrato. Now for me there was suddenly a grand design to the whole program. I could see that there are complimentary combinations of elements and a thriving life force, and we are all together. Salvaging The Future by Dean De Benedictis   Dean De Benedictis is a Southern California-based artist who has always utilized his interest in a variety of styles and cultures to enrich the quality of his musical expression. He aspires to communicate a similar functionality for the experiences of his listeners. Deans’ music is the result of his will to tie an essential common thread together between opposing genres and mentalities, as well as draw from them a natural sense of emotion, expanse and mystery. Sound exposes psychological truth; stripping ordinary objects of their normal significance, to create a compelling image that is beyond ordinary formal organization, in order to evoke empathy from the listener, with a combination of the depictive, the abstract, and the psychological.Driving into the complex, shape-shifting worlds that De Benedictis creates is always a magnificent adventure. He juxtaposes those frantic, glitchy granular textures against massive, cinematic spaces, sometimes he drops a rogue flute solo or harmonica right into a heavy electronic beat. It’s the kind of music that feels less like a collection of songs and more like a living, breathing, possibly dangerous ecosystem; De Benedictis has created an abstract, emotionally rich soundscape universe that rewards the listener.“My Salvaging trilogy of albums was a sincere and perhaps far-flung attempt to tie a form of common thread between the periods of my life and the electronic music I never released during those periods. Naturally, the reoccurring concept and eventual theme of ‘salvaging time’ manifested into the project. I basically have boxes filled with music like this, built up through decades. As such, my Salvaging trilogy was only one of many projects with a similar goal – to salvage works of the past – but the Salvaging Trilogy itself might be my most qualitative among them.“There are some very clear differences in style and approach contrasting each of these three albums, but it’s really the difference between the first album and the two albums following that one where the contrast is most visible. My first Salvaging album in 2005, Salvaging The Past, was a collection of work created throughout the ‘90s in my home studio, where I was surrounded by physical synthesizers and racks of outboard gear. Sometime between that album and the next one, Salvaging The Present, I acquired my first laptop and lots of appropriate software (more laptops would soon follow).“This changed the game, and my life, in ways that I couldn’t have imagined years earlier. I was already a traveler and an outdoorsman, so suddenly having the power to virtually access an entire studio within a little portable box was very liberating, conceptually and literally. I ended up travelling far and wide with the music, albeit mostly within US borders, but still found myself creating spontaneous productions in some of America’s most extreme natural environments. Over a period of about a decade-and-a-half, I lived a separate little lifetime of fair adventure with these devices, even including some uncomfortable brushes with death.“This spanned the length of both concurrent albums after the first one, I endured to keep creating through massive amounts of life changes and personal upheaval; through each new home I found, whether on-the-road or stationary; through broken alliances and rock-and-jazz-band breakups; through family drama and harddrive thefts and accidental overdoses, and of course a pandemic. Even through it all, my personal standard of innovation-balanced-by-emotional-sincerity never faltered, which probably explains the long lapses between Salvaging albums.“My desire to musically attempt going where no man or woman had gone before, both sonically and musically, remained. Everything from my sound-design methods to my processing methods to my performing and editing methods, was all totally signature, through every twist and turn and every new resolution. I suppose that’s what’s most noticeable and even distinguishable about this last and final album of the trilogy, Salvaging The Future; it’s the one with the biggest complexities and most contrasting styles, because my desire for balance between cutting-edge method and emotional sincerity were still unwavering through even the most tumultuous period of my life.”It is only natural, after all, to keep pace with scientific and industrial progress as well as follow the lure of pure psychic automatism, to stand for transforming the alienation which many people feel in the modern period, combined with the sense of reaching more deeply into the psyche, to be made whole with one’s individuality.With the completion of this trilogy, we acknowledge our part as a remote viewer of Dean’s life over three decades. Salvaging The Future—perhaps more than the prior two albums—is a restless collage, yet it is so well mixed that it lends itself to uninterrupted full-album listening. This listener is tuning in about 2x per day at the moment. Despite the challenges these decades have wrought, the trilogy’s close with “Our Story Survives Collectively” leaves us with a sense of hope. This is music for visioning. Salvaging The Future is available on Spotted Peccary Music. [Bandcamp] Salvaging The Future by Dean De Benedictis  The post Dean De Benedictis :: Salvaging The Future (Spotted Peccary Music) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Drumming for Yes for less than two years, having admirably taken over for the iconic Bill Bruford (who had left for King Crimson), Alan was suddenly vaulted into the limelight due to his place at la batterie for one of Prog's (and the world's) most opulent/visible/groundbreaking bands. After Yes' massive nine-month US and world-wide tours to support the release of their 1974 studio album, Relayer, the band decided to take a break to recharge. During this time each of the band members chose to express their individual ideas in solo album releases: Steve Howe's Beginnings on October 31, 1975; Chris Squire's Fish Out of Water on November 7, 1975; Patrick Moraz' The Story of I in the Spring of 1976; Jon Anderson's Olias of Sunhillow on July 9, 1976, and this album, Alan White's Ramshackled in March of 1976. To put together Ramshackled, Alan gathered his most trusted friends and collaborators of old (pre-Yes), many of whom he met while working with The Mark-Almond Band, Bell + Arc, live touring with Ginger Baker's Air Force or Joe Cocker, or an album he played on for Johnny Harris as well as a short-lived psychedelic band called Griffin back in 1969 in which White, Craddock, Kirtley, and Gibson had all played. Though I've owned this album for 50 years now, and always loved it (though I would never consider it representative of my preferences in musical styles), I am really looking forward to hearing it under the fresh spell of having gotten to know the earlier work of artistst like Alan Marshall, Peter Kirtley, Kenny Craddock, Bud Beadle, Steve Gregory, and Colin Gibson.Line-up / Musicians:- Alan White / drums, percussion, vocals, producerWith:- Alan Marshall (Riff Raff, Zzebra) / vocals- Peter Kirtley (Riff Raff, Zzebra) / guitar, vocals- Kenny Craddock / keyboards, vocals- Bud Beadle (Riff Raff, Zzebra) / saxophone solo, flute- Steve Gregory / tenor saxophone, flute- Henry Lowther / trumpet- Colin Gibson (Sanfu, Alan Hull) / bass, percussion- David Bedford (Mike Oldfield) / orchestral arranger & conductor - The Martyn Ford Orchestra / stringsAnd, special guests:- Jon Anderson / vocals (4)- Steve Howe / guitar (4)- Andy Phillips / steel drums (7)- Madeline Bell / backing vocals (8)- Joanne Williams / backing vocals (8)- Vicky Brown / backing vocals (8)1. "Ooooh Baby (Goin' to Pieces)" (5:32) an awesome funk tune from Peter Kirtley straight off the bat. It's driving, it's fun, it's funky, it's a cruisin' song! Alan's soulful LOU RAWLS-like voice (that reminds me of Arnaud Bukwald). Great album opener! Great Jazz-Rock Fusion. Really gets the blood pumpin'! (9.375/10) 2. "One Way Rag" (4:04) a great funk/R&B tune that sounds like Gerry Rafferty or Gilbert O'Sullivan singing (I'm assuming it's co-composer Kenny Craddock) and bounces delightfully with Colin Gibson's bass, percussion, Alan's drums, and, of course, Kenny's piano and organ play. Great contributions from the female background singers. (8.875/10) 3. "Avakak (aka Twelve Ways to Drink Meths)" (6:54) this is a song composed by Peter, Kenny, and Colin seen as "Havakak" on the Riff Raff album Original Man. The version the band records here starts out sounding like the intro to Roger Hodgson's "Fool's Overture" before Peter turns it with an "Awaken" opening riff and the band jumps in with a very odd funk-Yes-like syncopated chord progression over which soprano sax and guitar provide the jazzy lead melody in two revolving parts before things stop and start the song over using the full band to accompany Kenny's piano part until a quiet excursion into "Waiting Room"-like psychedelic percussive play takes over at the four-minute mark for about a minute before the odd funk-Yes-like motif retakes and Steve Gregory or Bud Beadle supply a flying treated soprano sax solo over the top of the oddly time signatured Jazz-Rock--and then a Yes-like door opens, someone lets out a scream, and it's over. An excellent, utterly exhilarating tune. I like this version (though it is very different from the Riff Raff one) very much. (13.75/15)4. "Spring - Song of Innocence" (5:00) gentle, soothing, soporific Hawai'ian-like music with some really cool and unusual instrumental sounds (thanks in part to guest stars Steve Howe and Jon Anderson as well as to Kenny Craddock's excellent keyboard contributions and Colin Gibson's expressive yet tender electric bass play) that make it sound as if it could have come from/been intended for Jon Anderson's Olias of Sunhillow album (which was to come out in July). (9.125/10)5. "Giddy" (3:11) a Jazz-Rock tune that sounds at first like Nina Simone's Sinner Man before Peter's lead guitar signals a clear Allman Brothers reference. Alan Marshall's vocal on this Kenny Craddock-Colin Gibson song is awesome, amplifying the song's Jazz-Rock elements marvelously (as does Colin Gibson's excellent bass play). So much fun! (9/10)6. "Silly Woman" (3:14) it's Reggae but it's so much more, it's Calypso, it's Ska, it's Afro-Cubano, it's fun and lively. Alan Marshall channels Joe Cocker, John Martyn, Van Morrison, and even Paul McCartney all at the same time. (8.875/10)7. "Marching into a Bottle" (1:59) acoustic guitar, flutes, orchestral woodwinds, and hand held percussion instruments create this quaint little anachronistic Neo-Baroque tune that should probably be on a GRYPHON or AMAZING BLONDEL album. (4.625/5)8. "Everybody" (3:13) Alan Marshall has really allowed his voice to evolve deep into the funky world of Soul/R&B as his Lou Rawls/Sly Stone, backed by some soulful female background singers, the song and its unusual vocal delivery remind me of something that might be done by Frank Zappa, Captain Beefheart, Eric Burdon, or Kaz Lux. I love how Alan and the girls bring it together for the choruses. And then explosion and it's all over! (8.875/10) 9. "Darkness" (5:35) yet another Gibson and Craddock composition, this one founded around a very cool swirling guitar arpeggio. The bulk of this jazzy, soulful R&B tune rests on the voice of Alan Marshall: in the first half it's anguished and insistent and then, after the orchestral break in the middle and Kenny Craddock's gorgeous classical piano play, it's Alan's achingly-emotional near-whispered vocal followed by, in the final 90 seconds, David Bedford's orchestral work over which trumpeter Henry Lowther lays down one of my favorite "goodbye" tributes of all-time. (9.125/10) Total Time 38:42A-/five stars; a minor masterpiece of eclectic Rock and Jazz-Rock compositions that are masterfully performed and rendered (with great passion and soul). Of the five Yes solos between Relayer and Going for the One, this has always been my second favorite (next to Chris Squire's Fish Out of Water.) After coming to know the background of Alan's band mates I am happy to confirm that that bias continues to exist. Highly recommended for lovers of eclectic Rock 'n' Roll and/or Jazz-Rock: just don't be looking for Yes music!

items.body: Review by greenpete — Closer to psych than what we know as prog, The Piper at the Gates of Dawn was released August 5, 1967. It is a surreal, slightly ominous title for a rock album. Surprisingly, leader Syd Barrett didn't conceive it. He borrowed it from his favorite chapter in his favorite book, Kenneth Grahame's fantasy classic The Wind in the Willows. But the title expertly sums up the mixture of science fiction and children's fantasy that inform the words and music on the record.Within these grooves we share English tea with all varieties of the phantasmagoric. Hallucinating gnomes. Existential scarecrows. Sinister, mind-reading cats. Outer (inner?) space denizens. "The doll's house, darkness, old perfume?"Ok, I hear you snicker. "This is the kind of airy-fairy stuff that gave hippies a bad name." You may be right. A lot of this stuff was done by hack musicians/writers eager to hitch a ride on the magic bus. But . . . Long before the Summer of Love became an innocuous clich� and marketing tool, there existed a few imaginative, English art students bent on taking music, words, and art to undiscovered areas. The blueprint for the new music was created by the band Pink Floyd, helmed by the youngest member, Roger Keith (Syd) Barrett of Cambridge, who named his band after two of his beloved cats (who were named after two obscure American bluesmen).According to his sister, Barrett had a rare condition called "synesthesia." Most of us only hear sounds and see colours. But some "synesthetes" can evidently see sounds, and hear colours. Barrett, a talented painter as well as musician, apparently exhibited this condition as a child and budding artist, years before he ever touched a hallucinogen.In early 1967, Barrett penned two eye-opening singles that titillated the London youth underground: "Arnold Layne," a true story about a Cambridge transvestite who stole women's underwear from washing lines; and "See Emily Play," a slice of English whimsy that teeters on insanity.Based on these singles, EMI Columbia financed Pink Floyd's first full-length LP. It was recorded in Abbey Road Studios, right when the Beatles were putting the finishing touches on Sgt. Pepper. Legend has it that the Floyd members occasionally peeked in on Lennon and McCartney to absorb the brilliance. I propose it was the other way around.If so, what might John and Paul have heard? There are two faces to this record: an unsettling and ragged trip into space (I'll call it the Gates of Dawn) and a pleasant and pastoral trip back to childhood (The Piper, and this would be all Syd). I'll save The Piper songs for later."Astronomy Domine" "Pow R. Toc H.," and "Interstellar Overdrive" come close to the later Floyd sound and were staples of the band's blinding, liquid-light-fantastic live shows. All soar into space on the static-y strings of Barrett's guitar. "Astronomy" is bolstered by Nick Mason's tribal drumming, and the 10-minute "Interstellar" by Richard (Rick) Wright's cosmic organ. "Pow R. Toc H.," one of the album's lesser songs, is an instrumental crammed with vocal and instrumental sound effects, but it has a characteristic spacey Floydian closeout.Let me interject that Barrett on guitar was no Eric Clapton. But he made up for technical inadequacy by bravely exploring the instrument's electric and aural capabilities (using a silver Telecaster adorned with 15 circular mirrors). He pioneered a technique of channeling bottleneck slide through an echo device, and it gave the Floyd a distinctive eerie sound.Back to the songs: "Take Up thy Stethoscope and Walk" is Roger Waters' very first composition. Nothing notable here except the paranoid vocals by Barrett."Lucifer Sam" is a sleek nugget about a third feline owned by Barrett, a mysterious Siamese named Sam. The descending chords and twangy guitar lines have been described as "psychedelic Duane Eddy," and recall the Sloan-Barri hit sung by Johnny Rivers, "Secret Agent Man." Sean Connery always pops into my head. It's the closest song to a "hit" single on the album, IMO.Now for The Piper part of the record: these songs were written exclusively by Barrett. "The Gnome" and "The Scarecrow" might as well be solo Barrett. I'm not sure if anyone else even plays on them, except perhaps Mason offering soft percussion help. Both are pastoral evocations that capture children's fascination with the unreal possibly being real. "The Scarecrow," also, has a rolling melody that may have made Paul McCartney blush while eavesdropping on the proceedings."Chapter 24" is a collection of observations lifted from the I Ching and set to music: "Change returns success/Going and coming without error/Action brings good fortune/Sunset, sunrise." This song may have been inspired by Barrett's interest in Eastern philosophies. Like other young people seeking new ways of thinking, he'd attempted to join a Sant Mat sect, but was rejected for being too young.The oddest song here is probably "Bike:" "I've got a bike/You can ride it if you like/It's got a basket/A bell that rings/And things to make it look good/I'd give it to you if I could/But I borrowed it." Note the rhyming, alliteration, and syncopation. Also, the little lyric twist at the end. On surface, the lyrics seem like nonsense. But Barrett was a skilled writer, and like all great writers, he understood the power of letters and words.Now for the pi�ce de r�sistance, the two songs that may be the cream of all English psychedelia. Musically and lyrically, they're a joy to listen to: "Matilda Mother" and "Flaming.""Matilda Mother" is a bittersweet memory of Barrett's about fairy stories read by his mother, with lyrics partly inspired by Anglo-French writer Hilaire Belloc, especially his 1907 parody Cautionary Tales for Children. The best psychedelic music was less about hallucinating through drugs than about transcending the mundane, and in "Matilda Mother," Barrett yearns to throw off the rigidness of adulthood and return to the comforting calm of his mother, and the "scribbly black" lines she recited, where the phantasmagoric was tangible, colours pulsate with life, and "everything shines." Rick Wright, the low-key, underrated keyboardist in Floyd, who later also wrote several evocative songs about childhood, sings the verse, while Barrett sings the slightly bitter chorus ("Oh, oh mother/Tell me more?")."Flaming" is my favorite song on the album. Originally entitled "Snowing," it's a tune that requires little effort to listen to, just opened ears, an open mind, and a willingness to float on "eiderdown" through fields of buttercups and dandelions. Listen to this with a good set of headphones and let Wright's deep organ fills wash over you, and Barrett's stirring multi-tracked vocals warm your insides. You may giggle at the sudden entrance of a cuckoo. But then, you're supposed to. On surface, this song is about playing hide-and-seek. We were all children, once, so who cannot relate to that? But, as Lewis Carroll, Kenneth Grahame, and Syd Barrett all knew, words have different meanings. This song is just as much about the exhilaration of being invisible, floating like a fetus, gazing at the hustle and bustle of a world gone cuckoo."Flaming" clocks in at a mere two minutes and forty-two seconds, but it's more imaginative than all four sides of The Wall. And it has one of the most beautiful musical closeouts ever devised. John and Paul certainly walked away shaking their heads in astonishment. It's obvious where they got the final notes for "She's Leaving Home."Many have tried over the years, but nobody writes songs like this anymore. Very few back then could, either.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — The Zzebra gang is benefitting from the boon that came in the form of keyboardist/composer Tommy Eyre, whose previous band, Riff Raff, had recently disintegrated. As the instrumental songs are being realized, Tommy convinces the band to bring aboard former band-mate Alan Marshall for some vocals. 1. "Panic" (4:34). a take-no-prisoners opener for the album, it speeds along at breakneck speed using a fairly simple template for its basic structure but then employing loud horns and a kind of choir-vocals approach over/within the peloton. It's good but it could have used something . . . more. (8.875/10)2. "You've Lost That Lovin' Feeling" (6:10) slowing it down to create a smooth jazzy cover of the iconic song first made famous by The Righteous Brothers. Nice warm electric piano from Tommy Eyre, nice presentation of the main melodies of the verses from the horns (Dave Quincy's soprano sax is key), and then guitar-led ramp-up for the chorus before giving way to Steve Byrd's acoustic guitar for the solo over the second verse giving way to sax and horns for the climb back to the second electric guitar-led chorus. At this time, the four-minute mark, the music kind of empties out, slowly, carefully replaced by a Eumir Deodato/Richard Wright-like passage over which a synthy-pan flute sound takes the lead in a very Jazz-oriented section. Mellotron and reverberating electric piano usher the pan flute to its finish as well as to the song's close. (8.875/10)3. "Karrola" (3:59) a repeating rapid-fire bass and guitar line opens this one, over which the horns and rest of the band present the rest of the layers of the song with Dave Quincy's alto sax taking the first solo over some power Jazz coming from John McCoy and Liam Genockey's driving rhythm section. Tommy's electrric piano and then horns and Loughty Amao's African vocal chitter-chatter fill the treble end of the next minute before the whole band converges to take us out with the main theme. Reminds me of both NUCLEUS and post-Third THE SOFT MACHINE. (9/10)4. "Liamo" (5:54) this Jazz-Rock Fusion tune feels as if the master tape of the previous song were taken down to half speed--which makes the legato lines of each of the instruments in the overall weave seem so slow and deliberate. Horns are very clear and deliberate while electric guitar and electric piano seem to dominate the fills and flourishes occurring over the top. In the fourth minute a chorus of vocalists seem to chant/sing an African-like line ("Liamo") while Steve, Dave, Liam, and Tommy continue to add their responses between the chant lines (in their breath pauses). The problem is that the vocal lines being slowed down as much as the rest of the plodding instruments, it feels as if the band is playing one of those exaggeratedly depressing New Orleans funereal processionals--only I keep waiting to hear the sudden shift (as the movies show it) into high-spirited music of celebration and elation. But, it never happens. The musicians more than prove themselves but the overall energy and feeling the listener is left with is more akin to big animal stomping. (8.75/10)5. "Death By Drowning" (2:58) Tommy Eyre is given some time to show off some of the applications his discoveries on his new electronic keyboards have revealed. In the third minute Dave Quincy joins him with some plaintive soprano sax play. Very Zawinul-esque. (4.375/5) 6. "Tree" (6:01) It turns out that the previous song was an intro to this one as Tommy's pensive pan-oscillating electric piano chord play opens this one before vocals and "distant" semi-muted soprano sax join in to sing about something metaphorical. Nice. At 2:18 there is a rather sudden and delightfully-welcomed shift into higher gear as bassist John McCoy takes off with some very animated racing funk play daring everyone else to try to catch him. Tommy is the most successful as his multiple keys are right there at the front of the pack but Liam and Loughty don't seem able as their sounds are left in the distance. Eventually, Dave's soprano sax convinces everybody to slow back down, which brings the team back to the opening motif for a vocal-led finish. Nice. Easily my favorite song on the album (despite its flaws). (9.5/10) 7. "Put A Light On Me" (4:59) clavinet! funky synths! Alan Marshall gets a truly lead vocal role in/over this one as John and Liam lay down an equally-funky rhythm track to match that of Tommy's keys. Alan is great though the band/producer still, obviously, don't trust him enough to give his vocal track appropriate front-and-center spotlighting. (How ironic that the lyric he's singing is about "put the light on me" as he finds himself not wanting to live in the dark! "I'd rather be on my own," he sings.) A catchy, memorable earworm of a song. Another top three. (9/10)8. "La Si Si - La So So" (5:12) opening with another great high-speed rabbit run from John McCoy to lead the way, everybody else is very quick to get in line, even Liam's drums, but more importantly, the horn section's accent blasts and, of course, Tommy Eyre's electric piano. (He's such a consummate professional!) The first true solo isn't launched until the very end of the second minute: it's Steve Byrd's searing John Tropea-like electric guitar, followed by Dave's tenor sax. They're both excellent and the rhythm section below maintains an awesome display of energy and togetherness. (Big shout out to percussionist Loughty Amao!) Great NUCLEUS-like finish to the album. A true Jazz-Rock Fusion classic! My other top three song. (9.75/10) Total time 39:47I have to admit to having higher hopes and expectations for this album--especially after just finishing the week of getting to know the output of the band RIFF RAFF--where Tommy Eyre and Alan Marshall previously spent some time. A-/five stars; a minor masterpiece of Nucleus-like Jazz-Rock Fusion led by some very skilled bass, sax, and keyboard players. Though there are some low points of inconsistency, the highs are respectably high. Recommended to all Jazz-Rock Fusion lovers.
