items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Sticking together for one more album, Roger Sutton's Riff Raff pull off another very cool Jazz Rock album--something edging its way into the Canterbury conversation. Perhaps working in Kent (where Canterbury lies) with producer Ken Burgess (who would go on to work with Tommy Eyre's next band, Zzebra) had something to do with that.1. "Original Man" (7:40) this Peter Kirtley composition opens with a one minute whole band intro that borders on sounding like something from one of their Canterbury contemporaries, but then in the second minute things settle down into a very cool almost downtempo ambient electric lounge music over which Peter sings in a bit of a Dylanesque style. Peter's lead guitar play in the middle portends the coming of Stevie Ray Vaughan as well as paying a bit of an homage to his contemporary, Eric Clapton. What a great, powerful song to open an album with! Signs of good things to come! (14.375/15)2. "Havakak" (6:06) another really cool Jazz-Rock Fusion song that sounds like something National Health or The Soft Machine would have done. There is just such a great warmth to the feel of this palette and the soundscape it creates: no matter if the band is ripping through it (first motif), slowing things down (second motif), blues-rocking it (third motif), or vamping for Peter Kirtley's extended solo (fourth motif), the sound just wraps around you and makes you feel a part of it. And to think it was a composition that Peter brought from working with keyboard master Kenny Craddock and bassist Colin Gibson during their Mark-Almond days! (9.75/10)3. "Goddamm the Man" (6:09) a Roger Sutton original places us in a juke joint in the Louisiana/Mississippi swamp as raw steel-string acoustic guitars pick away Jack Johnson style from both the left and right while Roger's funky bass and Aureo's drums and congas and Tommy Eyre's stanky electric piano and organ add and increase the funky stink (everybody seems to have taken on at least two tracks). I didn't think I was going to like this once it opened (especially with Roger's Swamp-style American White Blues vocals) but once it got going, once the background vocals and horn section's accents were added, the funk just took over: I'm a fan! (9.25/10)4. "In the Deep" (3:59) Oh, my gosh! Is Robert Wyatt in the house? Peter Kirtley's second offering to the album finds us deep in the forlorn ballad forms that reluctantly came out of the Canterbury Scene. There is so much funky R&B in this--and it feels so solid and natural! Every nuance and subtlety injected, added, and feels so perfect, so genius, so easy! Shades of two of the best to ever do this style: Paddy McAloon (Prefab Sprout) and Roddy Frame (Aztec Camera) as well as the contemporary master extemporaneosifier, Richard Sinclair. Awesome and alarmingly good! (9.75/10)5. "The Waster" (5:09) feels a bit like a continuation or variation on a palette, pace, and style used in all of the previous songs (the sound French downtempo band AIR mastered for their massive hit, >). Roger Sutton's second composition finds him drifting more into the singing style of Eric Burdon (think "Drink This Wine"; even the lyrical format is very much like that iconic song). I love the laid-back vibe of the musicians' spacious note and chord play, a late night application of funk. Horn accents, smooth Fender Rhodes, congas and drums, background vocals, bluesy rhythm guitar, lead sax in the instrumental section, nice, easy-going two-chord construct (think Traffic's "Feelin' Alright"). It's nice, it's fun, it's warm, it's equally well performed as the album's previous material, just a little more tranquilizing. (8.875/10)6. "Tom's Song" (4:22) the title, of course, referring to keyboardist Tommy Eyre, who is the composer of this song. Though it starts out having a little trouble defining itself and its melodies for the first minute, it eventually metes out some quite lovely music: the piano playing and synth strings support quite lush and romantic. Roger's bass and Aureo's congas are muted into the background leaving the synth strings, piano, voice, and Steve Gregory's weirdly-effected flutes in the foreground. Tom's vocal is rather gentle, doubled up, I think. It's obviously a sad love song about regret. I like it's edgy classical and jazz influences as well as Tom's genuine emotion. (9/10)7. "Speed" (9:16) another great construct from multiple influences: the funky blues, American Southern Rock, Traffic, The Allman Brothers, and a little Van Morrison and The Doors in the mix. Another Roger Sutton original, I consider this to be not a particularly great or memorable "epic" but definitely another serious and high quality rendering. (17.625/20)Total Time 42:41It feels weird to be categorizing music coming from Great Britain with labels like "Southern Rock," "Swamp Rock" or "American Southern Rock" but they would not be the only British artists attracted to those types of American sounds. (Think of Alan Parker's film The Commitments and its characters' connection to the Memphis Horns and the music of Wilson Pickett.) Almost every British artist who was coming of age in the early 1960s would cite American Blues, Soul, R&B, and even Jazz as essential foundations and inspirations for their music. Roger Sutton, Peter Kirtley, Tommy Eyre, and Bud Beadle would be no different. I do, however, give the band credit for hearing and emulating a bit of their own countrymates of the Canterbury Style.A/five stars; an eclectic and full-blown masterpiece of sophisticated and highly-nuanced original music by some sadly-under-appreciated musicians (and band). HIGHLY recommended to any professed and self-respecting music lover.

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 983"The Singles Collection Volume 1" is a compilation album of Queen that was released in 2008. It has tracks from all the first seven studio albums of the band. So, it has three tracks from "Queen" from 1973, one track from "Queen II" from 1974, five tracks from "Sheer Heart Attack" also from 1974, five tracks from "A Night At The Opera" from 1975, five tracks from "A Day At The Races" from 1976, four tracks from "News Of The World" from 1977 and four tracks from "Jazz" from 1978. It has also a non-album's track, a track that was previously unreleased on any of these studio albums."The Singles Collection Volume 1" has twenty-eight tracks. So, from "Queen" we have "Keep Yourself Alive", "Son And Daughter" and "Seven Seas Of Rhye". "Keep Yourself Alive" is an energetic piece, a straight forward rock song with different and unexpected changes in tempo, with great guitar and vocal work. "Son And Daughter" is a great hard rock song that proves Queen could make hard rock with quality and some progressive lines. "Seven Seas Of Rhye" is an instrumental track. Despite be a short piece is a beautiful song. From "Queen II" we have "White Queen (As It Began)". It's an acoustic ballad with a dark atmosphere, great lyrics, a nice melody, a great guitar solo and a good arrangement. From "Sheer Heart Attack" we have "Killer Queen", "Flick Of The Wrist", "Now I'm Here", "Lily Of The Valley" and "Tenement Funster". "Killer Queen" is a sophisticated and pompous art rock song with great vocals and chorus. It's one of their best songs. "Flick Of The Wrist" is a great track with nice vocals, excellent guitar work with an inspired riff. "Now I'm Here" is a song specially noted for its hard riff and great vocal harmonies. It's a powerful rock number with a heavy beat and catchy vocals. "Lily Of The Valley" is a short song with a nice melody that skills the great capabilities of Mercury as a songwriter. "Tenement Funster" is a good rock number with a heavy tune. It's one of the best Taylor's compositions, one who had stood better the test of time. From "A Night At The Opera" we have "Bohemian Rhapsody", "I'm In Love With My Car", "You're My Best Friend", "'39" and "Death On Two Legs (Dedicated To...)". "Bohemian Rhapsody" is one of the most known and the best songs of Queen. It's one of the greatest rock songs too. "I'm In Love With My Car" is a great rock song, simple and catchy. It's one of Taylor's best songs in Queen's catalogue. "You're My Best Friend" is a beautiful and catchy song with nice harmonies. "'39" is a superb acoustic ballad with great guitar work and beautiful harmonies. "Death On Two Legs (Dedicated To...)" is a great rock song with good harmonies, nice piano, amazing lyrics and a great vocal work. From "A Day At The Races" we have "Somebody To Love", "White Man", "Tie Your Mother Down", "You And I" and "Good Old Fashioned Lover Boy". "Somebody To Love" is a song with some complex harmonies and guitar solos and an incredible gospel choir too. "White Man" is a great hard rock song with excellent musical structure, strong melodies and guitar riffs, one of their heaviest tracks. "Tie Your Mother Down" is a good hard rock guitar based oriented song where May shines. "You And I" is a very simple beautiful song where the arrangements and performance of all band's members are great. "Good Old Fashioned Lover Boy" is one of the several music-hall inspired songs of Queen. It shows their humorous side. From "News Of The World" we have "We Are The Champions", "We Will Rock You", "Spread Your Wings" and "Sheer Heart Attack". "We Are The Champions" is one of the rock most recognizable anthems, even in our days. It's simply an amazing track. "We Will Rock You" is a great rock song that soon became one of the best known and most popular songs of Queen. "Spread Your Wings" is a beautiful rock ballad with good guitar harmonies. It's one of Deacon's better contributions to Queen. "Sheer Heart Attack" is a heavy punk rock song, probably the heaviest song that Queen ever wrote. From "Jazz" we have "Bicycle Race", "Fat Bottomed Girls", "Don't Stop Me Now" and "In Only Seven Days". "Bicycle Race" is a great song with an unusual chord progression with several modulations and multi-tracked vocals and guitar harmonies. "Fat Bottomed Girls" is a good rock song with an open tuning guitar riff based in blues and hard rock. It has also a great choral work. "Don't Stop Me Now" is a great song with great quality. It's one of their most popular songs even today. "In Only Seven Days" is a nice song with a good melody, good chorus and good musical atmosphere. "See What A Fool I've Been" is a non-album's track. It wasn't released on "Queen II". It was only released as the B-side of their single "Seven Seas Of Rhye".Conclusion: As its name indicates this is a compilation album only with tracks that were released as singles. This isn't a strange thing. As we all know, Queen was always a single's band with the releases of an amount of them. By the other hand, Queen never was a band with lengthy tracks. It has only singles that were released from their first seven studio albums. These are singles that belong to their best and most progressive phase. And I think it's peaceful to say the five first studio albums of the band have many progressive lines and the majority of the tracks that appear on "The Singles Collection Volume 1" were taken from those five albums. So, we can say this is a good compilation album of Queen.Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)

items.body: August 14th was another joyous evening in New Brunswick, New Jersey, which is quickly establishing itself as a hot spot for any touring noise acts to stop through on the east coast. Considering the enthusiastic attendees and diverse local talent pool available for these shows though, this comes off as no surprise. As a result, acts of both the new and old guard are able to use this intimate basement setting as a proving ground to show their stuff to a rather open-minded but critically thinking crowd. So when Midwest noisecore legends Penis Geyser announced they would be touring in celebration of their twentieth anniversary, booking them a show in Hub City was a no-brainer. First act of the night was FRICKER, who I would put into contention as modern noise’s best kept secret anywhere. The unique blend of digital soundscape smashing and crude feedback that he brings to the table can be tailored to just about any sound system that he comes across, which leads to each live experience being different from the last. Given the grimy nature of Ferren Mall’s sound system, I figured the crowd would be in for something on the crustier side of his material. Indeed, I was right on that front. Fricker spared no room for intricacies, and immediately summoned churning rumble grumble to suck the audience into a vacuum of unforgiving sound. The feedback drone that started the set eventually gave way to more variety in the chopping of digital samples, but never once lost its harsh backing. It seems like there is not a single sound system that this red-headed prince can’t conquer, and the audience seemed to think so, as much feedback I heard after was that this set made the travel and admission price alone feel worth it. With a bar set that high, things could only go up from there. When it comes to performances I take part in, I try to often gauge how the audience is feeling about things both during and after the set. With EVIL BONG, this task is never really that hard. Being showered in a sea of audience laughter and “fuck you” cries gives you a good idea of where your performance stands. With 6 members to this unit, every full band blast came closer to sounding like harsh noise wall than perhaps a noisecore band would sound. Between takes, microphone feedback would shriek like a drunken sailor beginning to hurl as song titles that took shots at New Brunswick, the audience, the bands playing and more came out of the mouth of their jackass drummer (side note: that guy really is a jerk). By the end of the set, with the audience in a frenzy, several members of the band just began to throw themselves directly at the audience. Hey, if hurting them emotionally won’t break their spirits, why not try physically?? By the time the band finished their crowd-pleasing closer, “Fuck Scronch,” there was simply nothing more they could do than to cheer and submit to the power of Evil Bong. Much like the film series this band was named after, audiences can’t help but find entertainment in the horror of this performance. To simply shower praise towards PENIS GEYSER would not be enough to describe the masterclass their performance was. While most seasoned attendees of noise shows expect short sets, nobody was expecting just 90 seconds from this touring unit. It’s 20 years of the band, you would be more than understanding if they wanted to play a long set. Nope; 90 seconds and it’s off the stage. But in that time, the band managed to whip the audience between blasting frenzy, tense restraint and dadaist rock n roll deconstruction that would have left the most seasoned of touring acts in absolute disbelief by how disciplined the trio were in their attack. While the blasting noisecore is what most of us came for, I found myself more intrigued by the moments in between, when drummer Mikeal VanCleave would gently tap on his kit while the string slinging duo of Brad Griggs and Charlie Mumma would treat their guitars as anything other than traditional songwriting. Strings were detuned, slapped around, beaten and mangled. The frenetic energy of these actions sounded closer to someone rattling their cabinet around than actually attempting to play anything musical. And when it all finally came to an end, it wasn’t bombastic. The band simply stopped playing whatever interlude they were in the midst of and started breaking their gear down. The audience cheered for an encore. I heard “One more! One more!” cried out repeatedly (what would even be “one more” for this band? Certainly not a song). Finally, one attendee walking out said “nah, it was perfect” and left. I couldn’t have said it better myself; a phenomenal band that could go on for another 20 years and probably still be as good. The new blood of New Jersey closed the evening’s happenings, as SPLOOGE RECEPTACLE came out with a table full of gear and the enthusiasm to inject their own brand of reckless abandon onto the audience. For those maybe not in the know, this group serves as the house band for New Jersey–based record label, NJMA, which has taken on the mantle of all things absurd and limited-edition in the Garden State. There are too many projects and releases to even begin listing the “essentials,” but Splooge Receptacle is where all these insane minds come together to celebrate the power of all things noise and core. Members were switching between duties on the mic, guitar, drums, electronics, etc. Really, if someone felt like they wanted to play something more than another member at the moment, they made the switch off occur. Similar to the Evil Bong performance from earlier, Splooge also engaged in their own form of audience antagonizing, as members crashed into the crowd while raging out through the wall of sound. Even when sound was not always perfect (sorry for providing a bad cable, team), their reckless abandon carried the set a great deal. With each passing set this group does, I become more and more excited at the prospect of where their sound can go. This group will be a name to look out for in the coming years if your listening diet tends to lean towards the more lo-fi ends of noisecore and shitnoise. So with the final blastbeat sounding off, the crowd took the streets, wandering off to who-the-hell-knows until the next show. Maybe some went to the nearest eatery available. Personally speaking, I went off to the Edison Diner for some late-night nachos with the Penis Geyser crew in tow. But maybe some walked away from this one thinking of how inspiring it could be to see the most chaotic and shittiest sounds performed so excellently. I know plenty that are still buzzing days later from the whole affair.

items.body: The Greek duo Incirrina, George Katsanos and Irini Tiniakou, formed in Athens in late 2017. On May 29, 2026 they released their third album, “Trace”, through the German label Cold Transmission Music on vinyl, CD, limited cassette and digital. Across three albums the pair have moved from darkwave towards minimal and electro-wave, built on analogue synthesizers, drum machines and Tiniakou’s vocals. I spoke to both of them about the record, the poet who writes their lyrics and what a two-person setup can carry onstage. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Trace by Incirrina Incirrina interview Q: “Trace” is already your third full-length album. Looking back on everything you’ve achieved so far, how do you view your journey as a band? And how would you describe and introduce this new record to people who may not have heard it yet? George: Indeed, after the releases of the albums “8.15” (2019) and “Lip Led Scream” (2022), we are happy to have our third LP “Trace” out by the label Cold Transmission, released 29.5.2026. We consider the band as a space for exploration, experimentation, personal expression, also as an inner journey and diving into our souls. Incirrina has brought us the joy of sharing our music with people across multiple countries. Until now we have toured in 12 European countries and played in many gigs and festivals, which led to beautiful and completely new experiences. Irini: In this album, we experimented with instrumentation, rhythm and vocal approach. We used a combination of analogue synthesizers, drum machines, octapad, electric bass guitar, electric piano and acoustic instruments such as kantele, waterphone, melodica. “Trace” includes 11 songs written between 2023-2025 in a 24-channel console, that belong in the genres of dark electronic, synth-wave and cold-wave. The minimal-synth and post-punk roots of our previous albums are still obvious, yet the new songs are enriched with dynamism, depth, and rhythmic diversity and we also explored new ways of delivering the vocals for this album. Also we would like to note that this album is the result of the collaboration of many people who put their heart and talent into it, and we are grateful to them – these people are Dimitris Dimitriadis (mixing), Anestis Psaradakos (mastering), uBuDancer (artwork, analogue collage), Nestor Theophilopoulos (photography), Maria Deligiorgi/Infrared Media (layout) and Suzy Hermann and Andreas Hermann of Cold Transmission. Q: If I’m not mistaken, you’ve been active for almost ten years now. How did Incirrina come into being, and how have both your collaboration and the band itself evolved over the years? George: Our common journey as Incirrina started in late 2017. Since both of us are professional musicians and music teachers, we’ve been involved in numerous bands and projects and music has always been the center of our lives, but neither of us had ever been in a purely synth band before. It was a great pleasure to discover already in our first meeting, in September 2014, that we had the exact same taste in music – we were talking for hours about Jean Michel Jarre, Joy Division, The Cure, Kraftwerk and numerous others… We became a couple, still the timing for forming a band wasn’t right yet – we were working hard in teaching and the other projects, and simply didn’t have the time to start something new together. But in 2017 life brought things together in such a way that conditions were created for something new to be born. Incirrina came into life with the aim to make music in the style we’ve deeply loved since we were teenagers. Irini: The first tracks were written right in our living room. Although I do write lyrics, we chose to base our songs on the poetry of William Blake, an artist we both deeply adore. After recording 6 songs, and without thinking twice, we uploaded them on Bandcamp (this was the first EP “8.15”, in December 2018), and suddenly something clicked. We received an unexpected wave of enthusiasm from complete strangers. Essentially, we started with no expectations other than making songs that we liked. It was magical how this evolved. One year later, in late 2019, the Greek label Geheimnis Records released “8.15” as an LP – the first 6 songs plus 5 new ones. Then COVID hit. During those strange years of isolation, we wrote the songs for our second album, “Lip Led Scream”, which was released by Cold Transmission in August 2022. One thing naturally led to another; some months before the lockdown, we had received an invitation to perform in Germany, in Slow Club Freiburg, a show that finally came to life in May 2022. That was the spark that started this beautiful adventure of European tours and live shows. In the years leading up to this year’s release of “Trace”, we focused on live performances as well as exploring new sounds and we also scored two theatrical plays in Athens. We are quite strict with our music, even though we compose new tracks very quickly, the ones we choose to release are very few (for every track we release, about four or five others are left behind). George: We really enjoy jamming and playing together, most of our tracks come alive through this very process. But there are also songs written entirely by one of us, then the other one enriched or reshaped them, regarding arrangement or structure. While we co-write the harmonic and melodic elements of our songs and handle the arrangements together, our individual roles are quite distinct. I focus on the rhythmic side, taking care of the live drums and drum programming, also the basslines and the riffs, while Irini handles the vocals. Q: One of the defining characteristics of your music is your use of analogue synthesizers. That seems like a very deliberate choice. What is it about analogue synths that continues to inspire you, and how has this aspect of your sound evolved over the years, particularly on “Trace”? George: Indeed, we have a great love for analog sound and analog synthesizers. Of course, there are plenty digital instruments we really like and also use. I adore Moog synthesizers, their rich harmonic sound fills the ear with very distinct frequencies. I love that you can never have the exact same sound. The instruments that I use do not have a “preset” or “save” possibility, so every time I make the sound from the beginning and I find this really thrilling. Analog synthesizers have personality; I feel like I’m using a sonic canvas when playing them, their sound has so many shades and details. Irini: We’ve used analog synths on all of our albums. In “Trace”, we paired them with acoustic instruments and also some digital synths, like the AKAI MPC and the Yamaha PS-55. Even though the Yamaha is digital, it’s from way back in 1983, and its sound has this nostalgic warmth that really speaks to us. Our relationship with instruments is just like with people… we have great chemistry and love for some, while others we just can’t connect with at all! An instrument is a whole world of its own, and a single sound can inspire an entire song. Some tracks started out just from a single sound, like the song “She Is In The Dream”. We also love building lots of layers and textures when it comes to orchestration, and our analog synths are perfect for mixing and layering in different ways. Q: Are you essentially a duo or more of a trio? I ask because I noticed that your lyrics are not always written by the two of you. Could you explain how that collaboration works, and how the lyrical themes develop in relation to your own musical ideas? Irini: Musically speaking, we’re definitely a duo; the two of us write and play all the music, and we handle everything that goes into running a band. But at the same time we also have a “secret” third member. This is the poet Konstantinos Londos, whom we are lucky enough to have in our lives as a very special and dearly loved friend. He wrote the lyrics for our last two albums (with the exception of two songs, one on each record). Konstantinos puts what we feel and want to communicate into words in the most wonderful way. Working with him is magical. A lot of times we’ll discuss a topic that’s really on our minds, and then Konstantinos will write a poem about it… and just like that, we have the lyrics for a song. Other times, we picked some of his existing poems that spoke to our hearts, set them to music, and turned them into songs (like “Mutate” and “Alien Room”). But either way, there’s always an incredible creative process between the 3 of us – we listen together to the musical ideas, discuss the meaning of the lyrics, how the words flow melodically, and their deeper impact. In the end, after plenty of changes and fine-tuning (and sometimes after a lot of tears) the song finally takes its true shape. Konstantinos has a rare gift for clarity, simplicity, humor, sensitivity and working together with him is really a pleasure. He is an explosive mix of a brilliant Renaissance man, a Homo Universalis, and someone who genuinely prefers to stay out of the spotlight. Q: Speaking of the lyrics, “Trace” is an intriguing title that can be interpreted in many different ways. The album also explores profound and, at times, rather introspective themes. Could you tell us more about the concept behind the album? And to what extent do the lyrics shape the atmosphere of the music, or is it sometimes the other way around? Irini: Finding the right album title is usually a tricky process, since it needs to capture a lot of different concepts in just a few words. But with “Trace”, things were easier – the title came about completely spontaneously from Konstantinos, right after a chat about what making this album meant to us. The word means “imprint”, and that’s exactly what this record is: the footprint of a collaboration between people trying to capture in sounds and words the things that spark their thoughts and haunt their nights. This is also stated in the album’s back cover: “Trace” is the imprint of “searching for wondrous, meaningful diversions, novel transformations and transitory acts of care and defiance”. Thematically the songs deal with the uniqueness of human experience and the struggle of not losing one’s inner freedom and individuality in dystopian times – the “seeming real” where all that is imposed and inhumane presents itself as the inevitable truth (“Always Here”). Celebrating diversity and self-expression, but always connecting and creating with other people, is a way out (“Mutate”). And the album itself is the result of such a process; we consider ourselves, against the odds, as artisans and friends who make music, share it and reinvent ourselves. Other songs cover universal, age-old themes like love, loneliness, the fear of loss, pain of death (“Sometimes”, “Region”), also the relationship with oneself and the connection with the world outside (“Diver”, “Find”), themes like the dream element, the urban landscape, and mysterious, fairy-like figures are touched upon in the songs “Alexia”, “Presence”, “She Is In The Dream”; burning issues of our time like domestic violence (“Alien Room”); and how the “self” connects with today’s world, showing endless introspection but a lack of empathy, human pain, and the way we try to hide it even from ourselves (“ΚΡΥΦΟ”, which means “Hidden”, the only track in Greek language). George: Since songwriting is a two-way street, as we described earlier, the atmosphere that is created depends on each individual song. When we start composing music for an existing poem, we are influenced by the content, the meaning of the lyrics, and the rhythm of the words and syllables. Conversely, Konstantinos would often listen to a musical theme we had composed and write lyrics over it, based on a topic that was on our minds and that we had been discussing. However, since the general vibe of our music and lyrics is already introspective and relatively dark, we take it for granted that we won’t stray from that… not out of principle, but because the darker element simply speaks to us emotionally and temperamentally. Q: How do you approach your live performances? More specifically, how do you translate the layered studio recordings, and especially the analogue elements, to the stage? George: Being a duo has a lot of advantages, like flexibility with rehearsals, the creative process, and traveling. But also has plenty of challenges… Practically speaking, if we wanted to perform our tracks live with their full studio orchestration, we would definitely need at least one more musician on stage. Our compromise is to use backing tracks for the drums, or a portion of them while I play the rest, and then we perform the melodic and bass lines live. We inevitably have to skip several elements from the album… still that’s not necessarily a bad thing for a live performance, because different things take priority on stage. Also, for gigs, we bring along smaller gear. It would be practically impossible for just two people to travel carrying the actual instruments we used to compose and record, so we adapt our sound to smaller, more flexible instruments, which are a mix of analog, hybrid, and digital instruments. When we play in our hometown, things are much easier and we can bring along some of the original (and heavy) instruments used in the recording. But when it comes to touring abroad, since we travel by plane and train, doing that would totally be out of the question for practical reasons. Irini: Over time, we’ve rearranged some tracks for our live shows to such an extent that they end up sounding quite different from the studio recordings, in terms of orchestration, tempo, and also vocals. This is especially true for songs from our first album. Also, since we love improvisation, we play the tracks a bit differently at almost every gig. We add intros, change up some riffs, and basically transform them depending on the mood of the moment. It would be really interesting at some point to make an album with our older songs exactly as they are played live, in a live recording setup. This happened already with one song, the “Only One Smile Alone”; the original one is “The Smile”, and following the suggestion of Andreas Hermann, we recorded it again in the way we play it live. Q: Finally, with an album title like “Trace”, it seems only natural to ask: what kind of trace do you hope this album, and Incirrina’s music in general, will leave behind? And what lies ahead for the band in the coming months? Irini: What we truly want with all our hearts is this: for people who will listen to our music, to feel something, to be moved, to dance, to feel good, or to find a personal meaning in our songs. Through our music, we aren’t seeking self-expression as much as we are seeking connection and co-motion, sharing in something as beautiful as music. We would love for the music of Incirrina to leave a small imprint of beauty in this world. Everything is fleeting and surely everything fades into the oblivion of time, but we would be incredibly happy if, even for just a few moments, we could bring joy to some people… just as we experience the joy of making songs and playing together, in rehearsals or in live shows. George: In the coming months, we will mainly focus on presenting “Trace” through live performances in Greece and Europe. We definitely want to work on producing some new songs as well, and we also plan to celebrate our 10th anniversary as a band with something special, which we will announce in early 2027…! Thank you for this interview, and we wish all the very best to you and your readers! Incirrina About Incirrina Incirrina is a dark electronic and minimal synth duo based in Athens, Greece, formed in late 2017 by George Katsanos (analogue synthesizers, octapad, drum programming, electric bass guitar, kantele, alto melodica, waterphone, samples, vocals) and Irini Tiniakou (synthesizers, vocals). The pair had met in September 2014 and were already working as musicians and music teachers in other projects before Incirrina became one of their own. Tiniakou first appeared as a guest vocalist on a release by the Greek act Metal Disco before the duo started releasing under their own name. Their first six songs, built on the poetry of William Blake, went up on Bandcamp as the EP “8.15” in December 2018. The Greek label Geheimnis Records issued “8.15” as an LP in late 2019, adding five new tracks to the original six. The digital maxi-single “Utter” followed in 2020, and in 2021 the duo shared a split maxi-single with The Man & His Failures, “Devastations / R.Daneel”, on Smash Records. Their second album, “Lip Led Scream”, arrived in August 2022 and was their first record for Germany’s Cold Transmission Music, which has handled their releases since. Reviewing it for Side-Line in 2023, Inferno Sound Diaries described it as “a pure Cold-Wave production which is sometimes reinforced with harder, EBM, elements” and “a well-crafted and fully enjoyable work without any single cut to throw away”. In September 2024 the duo returned with the double single “Immersion”, pairing “Presence” and “Alien Room”, again on Cold Transmission Music. Incirrina have performed in twelve European countries, including Greece, Germany, Belgium, Hungary and Croatia, with appearances at Plíísken Festival, Morphic Festival, Cold Transmission Festival, Death Disco Festival – The Warm Up, Athens Music Week, Metavasis Festival and the Athens Digital Arts Festival. Their live show began with an invitation to Slow Club Freiburg, a booking made before the pandemic that finally took place in May 2022. In the years between “Lip Led Scream” and “Trace” they also scored two theatrical plays in Athens. “Trace”, the duo’s third album, was released on May 29, 2026 on Cold Transmission Music across black and crystal-clear vinyl, CD, a limited cassette and digital. Its eleven tracks were written between 2023 and 2025 and recorded through a 24-channel console. Lyrics are by the poet Konstantinos Londos, except “Sometimes”, written by Incirrina. Dimitris Dimitriadis mixed the album and Anestis Psaradakos mastered it, with artwork by uBuDancer, photography by Nestor Theophilopoulos and layout by Maria Deligiorgi/Infrared Media. “Mutate” and “Always Here” preceded the album as singles, and “Mutate” was issued with a video. Side-Line’s review of “Trace” rated it 8/10. The duo say the next months go to live shows in Greece and Europe, with a tenth-anniversary announcement planned for early 2027.

items.album: Remembering Skinny Puppy’s Dwayne Goettel, 31 years after his death

items.body: Dwayne Goettel, keyboardist, sampling and programming specialist for the industrial band Skinny Puppy, died on 23 August 1995 at the age of 31. He was found dead at his parents’ home in Edmonton, Alberta, of an apparent heroin overdose. Thirty-one years on, Goettel remains one of the defining figures behind Skinny Puppy’s sound between 1986 and 1995. Dwayne Rudolph Goettel was born on 1 February 1964 in High Prairie, Alberta, Canada. A classically trained pianist, he grew up in Edmonton, where he played trumpet in his high school band before taking up piano and getting involved in the city’s small electronic music scene, including the groups Psyche and Water. He met cEvin Key in 1985 when Water opened for Skinny Puppy on their “Bites” tour. Key asked him to join the band the following year, replacing keyboardist Bill Leeb, who left to form Front Line Assembly. Goettel made his first contributions to Skinny Puppy on the album “Mind: The Perpetual Intercourse” (1986). His technical knowledge of samplers and studio equipment, particularly the Ensoniq Mirage, helped steer the band away from its early synth-pop sound toward the more abrasive, sample-driven style of “Cleanse Fold and Manipulate” (1987), “VIVIsectVI” (1988), “Rabies” (1989), “Too Dark Park” (1990) and “Last Rights” (1992). cEvin Key later credited Goettel’s early command of the technology, calling him “the master of sampling.” Alongside his work with Skinny Puppy, Goettel collaborated with Key on the side projects The Tear Garden, formed with singer Edward Ka-Spel, as well as Doubting Thomas, Hilt and Cyberaktif, which Key also shared with Bill Leeb. Goettel released solo material under the name aDuck and, in 1993, co-founded the label Subconscious Communications with Phil Western. Skinny Puppy’s eighth studio album, “The Process,” was recorded in Los Angeles beginning in 1993, but the sessions were marked by drug problems and conflict within the band. Vocalist Nivek Ogre quit in June 1995, and Goettel and Key returned to Vancouver with the master tapes. Goettel entered a rehabilitation programme in Edmonton before returning to work on Download, a side project he had started with Key. He was later readmitted to rehab. On 23 August 1995, Goettel was found dead at his parents’ home in Edmonton; his death was attributed to a heroin overdose. “The Process” was completed by Key and producer Dave “Rave” Ogilvie and released in 1996, dedicated to Goettel’s memory, as was Download’s debut album, “Furnace.” About Skinny Puppy Skinny Puppy formed in Vancouver, Canada, in 1982 as a side project for cEvin Key (born Kevin Crompton), who was also drumming in the new wave band Images in Vogue. Key recruited Nivek Ogre (Kevin Ogilvie) as vocalist, and the pair adopted stage names to avoid confusion between two members both named Kevin. The band self-released the EP “Back & Forth” in 1983 and signed to Vancouver label Nettwerk the same year. The EP “Remission” followed in December 1984, and Skinny Puppy’s debut full-length album, “Bites,” arrived in 1985. Bill Leeb, performing as Wilhelm Schroeder, joined on bass synth and backing vocals during this period. Leeb left the band in 1986 to form Front Line Assembly, and Dwayne Goettel replaced him, making his first contributions to “Mind: The Perpetual Intercourse” (1986). Skinny Puppy went on to release “Cleanse Fold and Manipulate” (1987), “VIVIsectVI” (1988) and “Rabies” (1989), the last featuring Ministry’s Al Jourgensen, followed by “Too Dark Park” (1990) and “Last Rights” (1992), the band’s final album for Nettwerk. In 1993 the group signed to Rick Rubin’s American Recordings and relocated to Los Angeles to record “The Process.” The sessions were affected by conflict and drug problems; Ogre quit in June 1995, and Goettel died two months later. Key and Dave “Rave” Ogilvie completed “The Process,” releasing it in 1996 in Goettel’s memory. Skinny Puppy reunited for a one-off performance at the Doomsday Festival in Dresden, Germany, in August 2000, leaving the keyboard station on stage empty in tribute to Goettel. The band reformed as a full-time project in 2003 with producer Mark Walk, releasing “The Greater Wrong of the Right” (2004), “Mythmaker” (2007), “HanDover” (2011) and “Weapon” (2013). In a 2023 interview, the band confirmed it had split up for good after more than four decades together. Goettel’s death on 23 August 1995 remains part of that history: 31 years on, his contribution to albums including “Too Dark Park” and “Last Rights” is remembered as central to Skinny Puppy’s sound.

items.body: Front 242 released the album “05:22:09:12 Off” on 23 August 1993 through Red Rhino Europe, with Epic issuing the record in the United States that November. The seventh studio album by the Belgian industrial/EBM group turns 33 this year. Its title is a substitution cipher spelling out the word “evil,” each letter replaced by its position in the alphabet. “05:22:09:12 Off” was produced and mixed by Daniel Bressanutti and Patrick Codenys alongside John Dubs and Eran Westwood, with Bob Ludwig mastering. The album marks the only Front 242 studio release built primarily around a guest vocalist: Kristin “99” Kowalski of the New York band Spill sings lead on most tracks, with Jean-Luc De Meyer appearing only on the remix “Melt (Again).” The CD edition runs 16 tracks, including “Animal (Cage),” “Modern Angel,” “Junkdrome,” “Serial Killers Don’t Kill Their Girlfriend,” “GenEcide” and “Crushed.” The album reached number 27 on the CMJ Radio Top 150. About Front 242 Front 242 formed in 1981 in Aarschot, near Leuven, Belgium, founded by Daniel Bressanutti (electronics, production) and Dirk Bergen (graphic design). Patrick Codenys (keyboards, programming) and vocalist Jean-Luc De Meyer joined in 1982, and Richard “23” Jonckheere (electronic percussion, backing vocals) joined in 1983 as Bergen moved into design and management. The band’s 1984 album “No Comment” was among the first releases to use the term “electronic body music” in its liner notes. Front 242 signed to Wax Trax! in the US in 1984, then released “Official Version” (1987) and “Front by Front” (1988) via Red Rhino Europe/PIAS, and “Tyranny (For You)” (1991) via Epic, its highest-charting album in the US. “05:22:09:12 Off” followed in 1993, released in Europe by Red Rhino Europe on 23 August and in the US by Epic that November. Drummer Tim Kroker joined for live performances in 2008. The band’s most recent studio album, “Pulse,” followed via XIII Bis/Metropolis in 2003. In 2023, Front 242 co-headlined the “Join The Forces” tour of Europe with Nitzer Ebb, alternating headline sets across dates including Berlin, Amsterdam, Oslo and Munich. Front 242 announced its farewell “Black Out” tour in March 2024 and played its final three shows at Ancienne Belgique in Brussels on 23-25 January 2025, retiring from live performance with a lineup of Bressanutti, De Meyer, Codenys, Richard 23 and Kroker. The live album “Black Out”, drawn from more than forty farewell-tour shows, followed via Alfa Matrix on 19 June 2026. “05:22:09:12 Off” now marks 33 years since its original release.

items.body: Brian Stillman is an American artist based in New York who is releasing his debut album, “Terminal Days”, featuring nine tracks. The album is politically engaged, with a raised middle finger directed at fascists, oligarchs, tech bros, A.I. fetishists, and human rights abusers. The music sounds like pure, good old-fashioned Industrial-Metal. The guitar riffs leave no doubt about it, backed by hellish rhythms and vocals loaded with rage. Despite the sheer power of this Industrial-Metal assault, there are also a few more refined Pop arrangements to be found. This makes the whole thing highly accessible, but believe me, the album remains packed with adrenaline from start to finish. There is a fine balance between the guitar work and the synths, creating a powerful and dynamic sound. Ministry fans will undoubtedly appreciate this project. “Terminal Days” sounds like a very promising debut album, and Negative Agent is undoubtedly a name to keep in mind. (Rating:7)-. Listen to “Annihilation Kick”: Annihilation Kick by Negative Agent About Negative Agent Negative Agent is the solo industrial-metal project of American musician Brian Stillman, who is based in New York. Stillman writes all music and lyrics and handles guitars, synth and percussion programming, sampling and vocals. The debut album “Terminal Days” was self-released on 8 April 2026 in digital, CD and cassette formats. Steve Wiener plays a guest guitar solo on “Mind Wipe” and Greg Schwan plays guest bass on “Pain Control”. The record also carries a bonus remix of “Fascist Beatdown” by Voidscan. Stillman mixed the album and designed the cover art; Hillary Johnson mastered it at Kale Shelter Studios. On the Bandcamp page for the release, Stillman states that “Negative Agent is 100% Human. No A.I. is used in any capacity, ever.” “Terminal Days” is the project’s first full-length and its first entry in the Side-Line archive.

items.body: Trying something new! Hello! This is going to be a bit of a different kind of post from what I regularly publish here on the blog. Actually, this is the first time I’ve ever really done anything like this, if I’m being completely honest. To those who managed to catch the August issue of the J-Music Advance Party over on my Substack, I talked about the amazing opportunity I had getting to speak with drummer Utsunomiya Kai of Saiwai na Heya in the lead-up to the band’s most recent album release at the time of writing, Sumiyaka na Kisoku. I initially reached out to the band hoping for just a word or two, but what I got in return was more than I could have ever expected, and something that I will forever be grateful for. One of the things that came out of our short exchange was the band very graciously taking the time to answer a couple of questions I had, both regarding the album and the band themselves. The idea at first was simply to use their responses as a reference for what I would eventually write for their Advance Party feature. However, upon receiving their answers, I couldn’t help but feel that it’d be a waste if I didn’t also share them with you guys. Not only for those of you who might already be fans and are curious to know more about the band, but also because I want to do my part in introducing Saiwai na Heya to as many people as I can who are willing to give their music a listen. As such, I went ahead and asked Utsunomiya-san if I could publish their responses here on the blog, to which I was graciously given the green light. It’s not the lengthiest of interviews, which is part of why I struggle to even call it one (lol), but I hope you guys find what the band had to say interesting all the same. So, with that little bit of context out of the way, please enjoy my conversation with Saiwai na Heya! About Sumiyaka na Kisoku (すみやかな気息): This is our first full-length album in a year and a half, following our first album, Sukoyaka na Shindai. There are unorganized spaces within individual lives, seemingly disconnected actions, and countless nameless everyday activities—things that, if deliberately written down and singled out as something “special,” might actually lose something in the process. When all of these things gather together into a larger whole, they naturally create currents and atmospheres of their own, which in turn influence the individual. This album takes the “city” as this kind of cyclical system as its central concept, portraying the subtle uneasiness hidden within everyday life from a different angle with each song.We consciously tried to weave into the album a sense of the breathing of people and light embedded within the noise and constant motion at the very heart of the city. It has become a fairly substantial body of work, so we hope you’ll take your time with it, sitting down with each individual song and discovering its particular character for yourself Leap：Regarding the album, are there any specific themes or ideas that led to creating Sumiyaka na kisoku? Like, when I listened to Sukoyaka na Shindai (your first album), it personally gave me the feeling of returning to my hometown after being away for a long time. With this album, is there any particular emotion or scenery that you hope listeners will imagine? Misa (Gt./Vo.)：In contrast to the suburban atmosphere of our previous album, this time we broadly centered the album around the theme of the “city.” The songs depict things like the actions and labor of individuals living there, as well as the ways those things interact with and influence one another. I reflected my own personal interpretation of what a “city” is in the lyrics, looking at it through perspectives such as the people who constitute it and the ways information circulates within it. Rather than simply trying to evoke a symbolic or stereotypical image of a city, I placed more importance on the process of contemplating the systems and ways of living that exist there; the labor, the people, and the interactions between them. So rather than trying to decipher some particular meaning from the album, I’d be happy if each listener could simply experience it from their own individual perspective and come away feeling whatever they personally feel. Leap：Musically, from the preview recently posted on X, I got the impression that the new album generally contains more up-tempo songs than the previous album. One of the things I particularly love about Saiwai na Heya is the beauty of the melodies, especially in the guitar and drums. Did you try anything new with the instrumentation or sound on Sumiyaka na Kisoku? Misa (Gt./Vo.)：For this album, rather than prioritizing a sense of consistency across the record as a whole, we focused more on bringing out the individual personality of each song. On “Interline,” for example, I used a semi-hollow guitar and deliberately aimed for a somewhat clumped, dense kind of guitar sound. On “Ishi,” we went for a heavier distorted guitar tone than we’ve used before, as well as doubling the guitars to give the song a harder impression. Kai Utsunomiya (Dr.)：As far as the drums go, with this band I generally try to keep the drum phrases as simple as possible and take an approach where they don’t assert themselves too much. However, in order to emphasize each song’s individual character and give the album more variety, I do think there are more intricate rhythm patterns compared with the previous record. I agree that there seem to be more fast-tempo songs than on the previous album, but at least at the time, I don’t think that was something we consciously set out to change. That said, when depicting the motif of the “city” on this album, I feel like that sense of speed ultimately ended up working to our advantage. In fact, personally, when we start creating new material from here, I’d like to approach songwriting with faster tempos and new kinds of structures that we haven’t used before as a starting point. Masaya Fujimoto (Ba.)：Compared with the previous album, while making this record I wanted to make greater use of the potential of what the bass can do within a three-piece band. I think that may be one factor in making the dynamic shifts stand out more clearly and giving the album a different impression. In terms of sound, while basically maintaining the balance among the three of us, there are also little bits of experimentation hidden throughout the record. On “Yūdō,” for example, I introduced an octave effect that we hadn’t used before. Leap：Could you tell me a little about the band? How did Saiwai na Heya form? Kai Utsunomiya (Dr.)：About a year and a half ago, I had a solo project where Misa helped me by recording vocals and guitar. We made several songs together, and needless to say, her technical ability was excellent, but I also felt there was something extraordinary about her sense for phrasing. My approach with that solo project was to immediately turn whatever demos came to mind into finished songs and release them one after another, so it had a very “instant” quality to it; more about quantity than quality. I started feeling that it would be a waste to simply consume Misa’s skill and musical sense within that kind of framework, so I asked whether she would be interested in starting something new together in the form of a proper band. By that point, I’d already joined and left quite a few bands, so I’d actually told myself, “I’m definitely not starting any more new bands.” But I decided to give myself one last shot and form this one. Then came the question of who would play bass. Misa is an exceptionally skilled musician, and I’m personally the kind of person who puts a lot of importance on a player’s technical ability, so, if I may say so, I wanted someone where we wouldn’t have to compromise at all in terms of musicianship. The first person who came to mind was Masaya, who had been my senior in the university jazz club. Honestly, I couldn’t really picture him playing in this kind of band, so I asked him without expecting much, but he happily agreed. You can already catch glimpses of his overwhelming ability as a bassist on the first album. That said, I still don’t think I’ve been able to create the kind of foundations in our songs that allow him to fully show what he’s capable of. Going forward, I’d like us to keep developing ideas that make better use of each member’s individual strengths, and eventually reach a point where the way we create music feels even more like the work of a band. Leap：And what are your musical roots and influences? There are moments when Saiwai na Heya reminds me a little of American Football. Have they actually influenced you? And are there other bands or artists that have contributed to your current sound? Misa (Gt./Vo.)：ASIAN KUNG-FU GENERATION and Spitz are constant influences for me. The Format is also my favorite band. I think they’ve influenced me not only in my work with this band but more broadly as well, particularly in how much importance I place on catchiness in melodies and riffs. Kai Utsunomiya (Dr.)：I like artists associated with the Zankyō-kei scene, such as People In The Box and Chouchou merged syrups., and I use them as references when creating music. As far as what this band ultimately puts out, once my musical tastes intersect with the different tastes of the other two members, the result tends to drift around the periphery of different genres, something that you can’t quite call post-rock or alternative rock. And to a certain extent, I’d say that’s exactly what we’re aiming for. At the same time, I personally love Midwest emo, and my roots are heavily influenced by American Football and TTNG, as well as emo scenes in Latin America, Russia, and Southeast Asia. The other two members don’t seem to have been particularly influenced by those genres themselves, but interestingly, I often hear similar nuances in what they bring to the band anyway. When I’m taking the lead on writing a song, I often try to make use of those qualities. Masaya Fujimoto (Ba.)：As mentioned in the story of how the band formed, in recent years most of my musical activities have centered around jazz, so while creating music for this band, I haven’t really had any particular rock bands consciously in mind. That said, I feel like I’m probably unconsciously influenced by Rush, whom I used to listen to quite a lot. If I were to name artists from other genres, I drew inspiration for this album from musicians such as Paul Jackson, Rocco Palladino, and Thundercat. Leap：(Lastly) How would you describe Saiwai na Heya’s music yourselves? Do you feel that it belongs more closely to a particular genre, or do you think of yourselves as taking a genre-less approach? Misa (Gt./Vo.)：I consider our music to be something that isn’t confined to any particular genre. The fact that each member comes from a different musical background is itself one of our greatest strengths. When we write songs, we deliberately avoid trying to steer them toward a particular genre. Everyone adds their own arrangements according to their own interpretation, so sometimes one particular genre might emerge strongly, while at other times different styles blend together. I think the element of chance that emerges through that process is another one of our strengths. Kai Utsunomiya (Dr.)：I feel the same. We don’t create music with the intention of fitting it into any particular genre. There may be a tendency for people to discuss us as an extension of the currently thriving alternative-rock scene, but we want to keep trying a broad range of approaches, drawing on a wide variety of interpretations. So in terms of our attitude or philosophy toward making music, I might describe us as a post-rock kind of band. Masaya Fujimoto (Ba.)：I also think genre is ultimately a result; a label that gets applied afterward, rather than something we consciously think about while creating music. At the same time, I don’t think any of the interpretations listeners come away with are wrong. So I hope people will enjoy the freedom and room the music leaves for their own interpretations. I hope to be able to do this again with other bands and artists moving forward. More than anything, I want what I say about the artists I feature here on the blog to be as reflective as possible of their own vision, rather than purely based on assumptions and speculation on my part. At the same time, I also think this could be another avenue for me to introduce these bands and artists to potential new fans, which has always been one of the main things I’ve wanted to accomplish with my writing in the first place. Looking back at the way I asked some of my questions though, I do realize that I might have been a bit too leading in certain parts, which I hope the band didn’t feel a certain type of way about. Again, I don’t normally do this, so that’s definitely something for me to keep in mind and improve on should I get another opportunity like this in the future. And speaking of which, if I do manage to line one of these up again, let me know if you’d be interested in seeing more conversations like this published here on the blog! Lastly, if you haven’t yet, please check out Saiwai na Heya’s latest album Sumiyaka na Kisoku! And if you want to support the band, do consider picking up a physical copy. They offer international shipping through BASE and Bandcamp. If you choose the latter, keep in mind as well that during Bandcamp Friday, all proceeds from your purchase go directly to the band! Happy Listening!

items.body: ちょっと新しいことに挑戦！ こんにちは！今回は、普段このブログで公開しているものとはちょっと違った記事になります。というか、正直に言うと、こういうことをやるのは今回が本当に初めてだったりします。 Substackの「J-Music Advance Party」8月号を読んでくださった方ならご存じかもしれませんが、そこで少しお話しした通り、記事執筆時点でのさいわいな部屋の最新アルバム『すみやかな気息』のリリースに先駆けて、ドラマーの宇都宮海さんとお話しするという、とてもありがたい機会に恵まれました。最初にバンドへ連絡したときは、ほんの一言二言でもお話を聞けたら、くらいの気持ちだったのですが、実際に返ってきたものは自分が想像していた以上のもので、これからもずっと感謝し続けるだろうなと思えるような経験になりました。 その短いやり取りの中で、ありがたいことに、アルバムについて、そしてバンドそのものについて、自分が気になっていたいくつかの質問にもメンバーのみなさんが丁寧に答えてくださいました。当初は、その回答をAdvance Partyでさいわいな部屋を紹介する際の参考にさせていただくつもりでした。 でも、実際に回答をいただいてみると、これを自分だけのところに留めて、みなさんにも共有しないのはあまりにももったいないな、と。 すでにさいわいな部屋のファンで、もっとバンドのことを知りたいと思っている方にはもちろんですが、それだけではなく、まだ彼らの音楽を知らない方にも、これをきっかけに聴いてもらえたら嬉しい。自分自身、さいわいな部屋の音楽を一人でも多くの人に知ってもらうために、できることをしたいと思ったんです。 そんなわけで、宇都宮さんに「いただいた回答をブログでも公開していいですか？」とお願いしてみたところ、ありがたいことに快くOKをいただきました。 決してものすごく長いインタビューというわけではなくて、そもそも自分でもこれを「インタビュー」と呼んでいいのかちょっと迷っているくらいなんですが（笑）、それでも、さいわいな部屋のみなさんが話してくださったことを、みなさんにも楽しんで読んでいただけたら嬉しいです。 というわけで、前置きはこのくらいにして―― さいわいな部屋とのお話を、ぜひお楽しみください！ 『すみやかな気息』について 前作の1stアルバム『すこやかな寝台』から1年半ぶりとなる、新作フルアルバムです。特別に書き留めてしまえばかえって取りこぼされてしまう、整頓されていない個人の余白や脈絡のない行動、そんな名もない営みが集まり形成された大きな集合は、ひとりでに潮流や気配を作り出し、また個人へと影響を与えます。このような循環するシステムとしての「都市」を本作のコンセプトとして据え、日常に潜むささやかな不穏さを、楽曲ごとに異なる角度から描いています。都市ど真ん中の喧騒や忙しなさに組み込まれた、人や光の呼吸を感じられるタッチを、意識して織り込んでいます。かなりのボリュームを持った作品になりましたので、じっくりと腰を据えて一曲ずつ味わいを確かめながらお聴きいただけますと幸いです。 Leap：まずアルバムについてです。『すみやかな気息』を制作するにあたって、何かテーマやコンセプトのようなものはあったのでしょうか？ 個人的な話になりますが、『すこやかな寝台』を聴いたとき、自分は「久しぶりに故郷へ帰ってきたような感覚」を覚えました。どこか安心感があって、とても居心地のいい作品だと感じています。今回のアルバムでは、リスナーに何か特定の感情や景色を思い浮かべてもらいたい、というようなイメージはありますか？ (Gt.Vo.みさ) 前作の都市郊外的な雰囲気と対比し、大きく「都市」というテーマで制作しました。そこで営まれる個人の行動や労働、それらが及ぼす相互作用のようなものを描いています。 個人的に解釈した「都市」というものを、それを形作る人のありかたや情報の回り方といった視点から歌詞に反映しています。単に記号的な都市のイメージを彷彿とさせる目的よりも、そこにある労働や人々、その相互作用など、その仕組みやある種暮らしに思いを馳せる過程を重視して書いたので、何かを読み取ろうとするよりも、聴く人もそれぞれ個人的な視点のまま何かしらを感じていただけたら嬉しいです。 Leap：また音楽的な面でも、最近Xで公開されていた試聴を聴いていて感じたのですが、新作は前作よりも全体的にテンポの速い楽曲が多い印象を受けました。自分はさいわいな部屋の、特にギターとドラムを中心としたメロディの美しさが本当に好きなのですが、『すみやかな気息』では楽器アレンジやサウンド面で何か新しい挑戦もされているのでしょうか？ (Gt.Vo.みさ) 今作では全体の統一感よりは、曲ごとの個性を際立たせるような音作りを意識しました。「インターライン」ではセミアコであえてダマっぽいギターを意識してみています。「石」では、これまでにない重めの歪んだギターサウンドやダブリングでハードな印象を与えるようにしたりしています。 (Dr.Kai Utsunomiya) ドラムについて、このバンドでは極力ドラムフレーズはシンプルに、主張しすぎないアプローチを取ろうと考えて制作しています。ですが、楽曲の個性を際立たせてバリエーションを持たせるために、前作と比べると込み入ったリズムパターンが増えているかなとは思います。確かに前作よりも曲のテンポが早いものが増えた印象はありますが、今のところ意識的に変えたつもりはありませんでした。しかし今作で「都市」というモチーフを描く際に、テンポの速い印象が結果的にプラスに作用している気はしています。むしろ今後新たに制作をする時に、今までに無い早いテンポ・新しい構成を前提として曲作りを進めていきたいなと、個人的には考えています。 (Ba. Masaya Fujimoto) 今作では前作と比べるとより3ピースにおけるベースという役割のポテンシャルを活かそうという思いを込めながら制作を進めてきました。それがより緩急を際立たせ、新たな印象を抱かせる要因の一つになっているのかなと思います。サウンド面では基本は3者のバランスを保ちつつも「誘導」では新たにオクターブエフェクトを採用していたりと密かに遊びを取り入れた作品になりました。 Leap：そして、バンドについてもぜひ少し教えていただけたら嬉しいです。さいわいな部屋はどのような経緯で結成されたのでしょうか？ (Dr.Kai Utsunomiya) 1年半ほど前に、元々私のソロプロジェクトという形でみささんに歌・ギター入れをお手伝いいただいていたことがあります。数曲一緒に作らせてもらったのですが、演奏力は言わずもがな、フレージングのセンスにも非凡なものを感じていました。こちらのソロプロジェクトは、思いついたDEMOをすぐさま形にしてどんどんリリースする方針だったので、質より量で勝負のインスタントな側面が強かったです。みささんのスキルとセンスをこの形で消費してしまうのは勿体無いと感じたため、ぜひバンドという形で新しく進めてみないかということで打診しました。 私はそのとき既にバンドをかなりの数抜けたり組んだりしてきていたので、もうこれ以上新規バンドは増やさないぞと考えてはいたのですが、泣きの一回という形で組ませてもらうことになりました。 ベースを誰にするかというところですが、みささんのスキルが卓越しているかつ私自身かなりプレーヤーのスキル面を重視するタイプなので、技術的に妥協のない人選にしたいなと僭越ながら考えていました。最初に思い当たったのが大学時代ジャズ研の先輩であったまさやさんで、正直あまりこのようなバンドで演奏しているイメージがなかったのでかなりダメもとで声をかけてみたところ、快く引き受けてくれました。1stアルバムの制作でもその圧倒的なベーススキルの片鱗が垣間見得ています。ただ、まだ彼の本領を完全に発揮できるような曲の土台作りをできていない気がしているため、これからさらにメンバーの持ち味を活かせるようなアイデア出しを進めていき、さらに「バンドらしい」制作ができている状態に持っていきたいと考えています。 Leap：また、音楽的なルーツや影響を受けたアーティストについてもお聞きしたいです。自分は、さいわいな部屋の音楽を聴いているとAmerican Footballを少し思い出す瞬間があるのですが、実際に影響を受けていたりするのでしょうか？もし他にも現在のサウンドに繋がっているバンドやアーティストがいれば、ぜひ教えていただけたら嬉しいです。 (Gt.Vo.みさ) ASIAN KUNG-FU GENERATIONとスピッツの影響は常にあります。またthe Formatが一番好きで、メロディやリフなどにキャッチーさを重要視する点としてバンド活動に限らず影響を受けていると思います。(Kai Utsunomiya)People In The BoxやChouchou merged syrups.など残響系のアーティストが好きで、制作においてリファレンスとしています。このバンドのアウトプットとしてはメンバー二人の異なる音楽的趣向と交わることでポストロックともオルタナとも言えない周辺的なジャンルを漂う結果となっており、それはある程度狙い通りであるとも言えます。 また一方、私個人としてはmidwest emoがとても好きで、ルーツとしてAmerican FootballやTTNG、ラテンアメリカやロシア、東南アジアのemoシーンからの影響をかなり受けています。メンバー二人のルーツとしては特にそのあたりのジャンルから大きな影響を受けている訳ではなさそうなものの、もらうアウトプットには近しいニュアンスが感じ取れることも多く、私主導で作る曲についてはそこを活かして制作している場合も多いかと思います。 (Ba. Masaya Fujimoto)前述の結成経緯にもある通り、自分は近年ジャズを中心とした活動をしていたため、制作活動を行う中で特定のロックバンドを意識していることはあまりなかったです。ただ、以前よく聴いていたRushからは無意識的に影響を受けている気がしますし、他ジャンルのアーティストで挙げるならば、今作はPaul JacksonやRocco Palladino、Thundercatなどからヒントを得ています。 Leap：(最後に)さいわいな部屋の音楽をご自身ではどのように表現されますか？特定のジャンルに近いという感覚があるのか、それともジャンルにとらわれない音楽だと考えているのか、そのあたりのお話もぜひ伺ってみたいです。 (Gt.Vo.みさ) 私たちの音楽は、特定のジャンルにとらわれないものだと考えています。メンバーそれぞれが異なるルーツを持っていること自体が、私たちの大きな強みです。楽曲制作の際も、あえて特定のジャンルに寄せることはしません。全員が独自の解釈でアレンジを重ねるため、時には一つのジャンルが濃く現れることも、融合することもあります。その過程で生まれる偶然性も強みの一つだと思います。 (Dr.Kai Utsunomiya) 同上で、特定のジャンルに当てはめた制作はしていません。盛り上がっているオルタナティブロックシーンの延長として語られやすい部分もあるかもしれませんが、とにかくバラエティに富んだ解釈で幅広いアプローチを試みていきたいと考えているので、スタンスとしてはポストロック的なバンドであると言いたいかもしれません。 (Ba. Masaya Fujimoto)自分もジャンルに関しては「結果」として後からラベリングされるものであって、制作においてはそれを意識することはありません。ただし、リスナーの皆さんがそれぞれ抱く「解釈」はどれも間違いではないと思うので、その解釈の余地を是非楽しんでいただければと思います。 今後も、こういうことを他のバンドやアーティストの方々とまたできたらいいなと思っています。何より、このブログでアーティストについて書くとき、自分の勝手な推測や憶測だけで語るのではなく、できる限り本人たちが思い描いているものや、その音楽に込めた考えを反映した内容にしたいと思っているからです。 それと同時に、こういった形で直接お話を聞くことも、まだ彼らのことを知らない新しいリスナーにバンドやアーティストを紹介するための、また一つの方法になるんじゃないかなとも思っています。そもそも、自分がこうして音楽について書き続けている大きな理由の一つが、それだったりするので。 ただ、改めて自分がした質問を振り返ってみると、ところどころ少し誘導的すぎたかもしれないな、とも思っています。バンドのみなさんが変なふうに感じていなければいいのですが……。こういうことは普段やっていないので、もしまた同じような機会に恵まれたら、そのあたりは自分自身もっと意識して、改善していきたいところですね。 そして、まさにその話なんですが、もしまたこういった機会を作ることができたら、今回のような「会話」をこのブログで読んでみたいか、ぜひみなさんの意見も聞かせてください！ 最後に、まだ聴いていないという方は、ぜひさいわいな部屋の最新アルバム『すみやかな気息』をチェックしてみてください！そして、バンドを応援したいという方は、ぜひCDなどのフィジカル版を手に取ることも検討してみてください。BASEとBandcampから海外発送にも対応しています。Bandcampを利用する場合は、Bandcamp Fridayに購入すると、購入代金がすべて直接バンドに還元されるということも、ぜひ覚えておいてください！ Happy Listening!

items.excerpt: By the time Syna Awel reaches “Incantation”, the sun has dropped. It closes an open-air acoustic session she filmed in a single afternoon this year, five Amazigh songs in a row, the last easing into a jam as the daylight goes. She is Franco-Algerian, a singer and percussionist who grew up in Aït Bouaddou, a village in the Kabyle mountains of northern Algeria. Her songs come out of Amazigh oral tradition, poetry and melody carried by voice, and she brings them into contemporary jazz.
items.body: By the time Syna Awel reaches “Incantation”, the sun has dropped. It closes an open-air acoustic session she filmed in a single afternoon this year, five Amazigh songs in a row, the last easing into a jam as the daylight goes. She is Franco-Algerian, a singer and percussionist who grew up in Aït Bouaddou, a village in the Kabyle mountains of northern Algeria. Her songs come out of Amazigh oral tradition, poetry and melody carried by voice, and she brings them into contemporary jazz. For the session she sings with Luc Lavenne on guitar, Anis Agrebi on oud, Tony Sgro on derbouka and Mahir Bostandzija on percussion. Where the album set her voice against jazz piano and bendir, this acoustic line-up answers with oud and hand percussion. Awel sings “Incantation” in Kabyle. The line “Kul yiwen yesɛa tidet-ines” means everyone holds their own truth, and the next line adds that everyone does what they can. She sets that against the turning of a day: the sun sets, the moon takes the evening, and it all comes round again. The songs come from Awel, her 2024 debut, arranged by drummer Karim Ziad and released on Imago Records. The full session, subtitled in Kabyle and French, plays on her YouTube channel. Stream “Incantation” HERE and get your copy of Awel following THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: Syna Awel – Incantation (Acoustic Live Session) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.
